speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REDUCTION IN EXCISE TAX-ENCOURAGEMENT OF DOMESTIC BEET SUGAR PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I should like to make a statement on the subject of sugar. The increased cost of raw cane sugar, the necessity of rationing supplies-of sugar both for household and industrial uses, and the desirability of encouraging the production of domestic beet sugar in the present emergency, have necessitated certain changes in the sugar situation which I would' like to explain to the house.
As the house is aware, our purchases of cane-sugar are made for the joint account of the United Kingdom and Canada by the British ministry of food. From the beginning of the war they have purchased for our joint account the total exportable surplus of British empire countries. The contracts are on an f.ob. place of shipment basis and in the present calendar year the cost of such British empire sugars has been increased by 1 to 14 shillings per hundredweight. War risk insurance costs have substantially increased and freights will no doubt average higher during the present year. Approximately one-third of imported sugars have -been drawn from countries outside the empire. Last year these were purchased at an extraordinarily low price. They are mainly from Cuba and Santo Domingo, and the cost of such sugars in the present year will be $2.65 U.S. currency per one hundred pounds f.o.b. country of shipment, which is an increase of almost 14 cents per pound as compared with last year. All imported sugars are sold by the sugar administrator at a fixed price c.i.f. refineries. This price has been held unchanged since May, 1940, at the figure of $3.30 per one hundred pounds. It is now proposed to increase this price to $3.55 and to increase the refiner's margin between his cost of raw sugar and the net selling price for refined sugar by about 21 cents per one hundred pounds. In this connection it may be noted that there has been no change in refiners' margins since control was established at the outbreak of war and the margin allowed has been below the margins obtained by refiners in the pre-war years in

Wool
spite of the substantial increases in cost that have taken place. These increases in operating costs will now be further aggravated by the reduced volume of production necessitated by the rationing of sugar.
Under existing circumstances, relating to accessible supplies and shipping difficulties, it is obviously in the country's interests that the maximum amount of domestic beet sugar should be produced, and the sugar administrator some time ago notified all beet sugar producing companies that they should do everything possible to stimulate production. The increased value of about one-half cent per pound in refined cane sugar will of course extend to beet sugar and, in addition, contributions which have been made in the past to the sugar administrator to equalize the net price with the cost of cane sugar have been discontinued. This will result in an increased gross to the beet sugar factories of 83J cents per one hundred pounds of refined sugar.
The proportion of this increased value which will go to the beet farmers will, of course, vary on account of different terms of contracts with different factories and also as a result *of differences in yields of tonnage and sucrose of the beets, but will amount, I am advised, even under the most unfavourable circumstances, to over SI per ton in the price of sugar beets.
The new factory in Manitoba had an unfortunate experience last year. First, harvesting was interfered with by unusual rains, and an unusually early closing in of winter resulted in about one-quarter of the crop being left in the ground. With a considerable increase in the production in Alberta and normal expectations in Manitoba, it is anticipated that the production of beet sugars in these two provinces may slightly exceed the total requirements at the reduced rate of consumption of the three prairie provinces. Soft or brown sugars and other specialties are not made by the beet sugar factories, and some manufacturing processes require cane sugar. Therefore it seems probable that a considerable quantity of beet sugar from the prairies will be marketed outside that area. Prospects of an increase in Ontario beet sugar production are somewhat obscure, due principally to a shortage of labour. The departments of agriculture and labour are, I believe, studying this question with a view to possible relief.
On the recommendation of the wartime prices and trade board, we are taking certain steps to ensure that the above adjustments may not affect the price of sugar to the public. In the budget resolutions we shall propose a reduction in the excise tax on sugar from 2 cents to 1\ cents per pound. Pending such formal action, we are providing for a remission of this tax to the extent of one-half
cent per pound dating from yesterday, February 16. This remission of a part of the excise tax has, as I have said, been necessitated by the desire to avoid any increase in the cost of sugar to the public. To prevent the realization of any inventory profits, one-quarter cent per pound will be collected on all inventories in the hands of the refineries as at the close of business on February 14.

subtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASED ALLOWANCE BY BRITISH COLUMBIA GOVERNMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASED ALLOWANCE BY BRITISH COLUMBIA GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The other day the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) asked a question about old age pensions in British Columbia. I replied in a way which I find was not as complete or precise as it should have been. The hon. member asked whether the Canadian government by order in council had amended the old age pension regulations so that the increased pen-

sion being paid by the government of British Columbia will not involve a corresponding reduction on the part of the federal government, and also whether I could tell him what was "the immediate situation in British Columbia."
In regard to the first of these questions, I said at the time that I believed we had communicated with all the provinces with regard to such an amendment of the regulations, but that I did not know what replies had been received. Actually I find that we have not communicated with all the provinces but have instead been relying upon the statement I made in the house on November 14 last, to the effect that if any of the provinces desires us to take the necessary steps to allow a province to pay a supplemental pension without such payment affecting the maximum pension now payable under the present act and regulations, "the government is prepared to amend the regulations and, if necessary, the act, to ensure such supplementary payments by a province do not entail a reduction in the pension payable under the act." I find also that when one province raised this question during the meeting with representatives of provincial governments in December last, I again stated the dominion's position directly to all the provinces in substantially the same words as I used in November last.
The situation, therefore, is that if and when we receive a formal request from any province to amend our regulations in this respect, we shall be glad to make the necessary amendment. For some time it was not clear to me whether an amendment to the regulations would be sufficient or whether the act itself had to be amended. I am now advised by the Department of Justice that an appropriate amendment to the present regulations could be made under the power given in the act itself, to provide by regulation for the manner in which the income of a pensioner is to be determined for the purpose of the act.
In regard to the second question asked by the hon. member for Acadia, I find that the Premier and Minister of Finance of the province of British Columbia made the following statement in his budget speech delivered on January 23:
The government of the province has given careful consideration to this matter and is of the opinion that conditions in British Columbia warrant the increase of old age pensions to $30 per month, and, pending appropriate action by the dominion to that effect, it proposes to supplement the pension now paid by $5 per month. Of this amount, $2.50 is the provincial share of the increase recommended, and the other $2.50 represents a war-time cost of living bonus, which will cease if the scale of pensions is increased by the dominion before the cessation

Privilege-Mr. Poidiot
of Hostilities. The payment of this additional sum will be made on precisely the same basis as current pensions and will be subject to the maximum limitation provided in the act. Generally speaking, a British Columbia pensioner will now receive $25 instead of $20 per month. Should the supplemental payment, however, bring the total income above the maximum of $365 per annum, it will be reduced by that portion which would be in excess of the said maximum.
This statement apparently represents the present policy of the government of that province. I understand that an item was included in the estimates to provide the necessary appropriation for this supplemental pension, and as the provincial legislature has adjourned, the presumption is that the item was passed. I expect, therefore, that we will shortly be receiving a formal request from the province of British Columbia asking us to take any steps that may be necessary to make it possible for the province to implement its policy. I may add that if I understand correctly what the provincial government intends it may not be necessary for us to make any amendment even to the regulations, because you will note from the statement I have read from Mr. Hart's budget speech that the supplemental pension is only to be given in cases of pensioners who have supplemental income-that is, income above a maximum pension payable under our act of $20 per month-of less than $125 per year, and is only to be given in such cases to such an amount up to $5 per month as will bring the total income, including present pension, provincial supplemental pension and any supplemental income, to an amount not in excess of $365 per year.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, February 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Alphonse Fournier for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the opening of this session parliament has been seeking which one of two path opening out before it will lead straight to the objective, which is victory and the establishment of a 'better order. This pause is not a waste of time. Indeed, effective action stems from thought which directs.
By what principles should this search be guided? In the first place, this war is a conflict between two ways of life, a conflict from which no people is free. All nations, in varying degrees, are shaken by it. In such a conflict, to seek refuge in indifference is equivalent to desertion. Either our civilization will perish or hitlerism, slavery and iniquity will be vanquished.
From this principle there flows a fundamental consequence: each country is fighting for itself. England, Russia, the United States, China, Canada are waging war each one for its own preservation. Canada, therefore, is not fighting for the triumph of England or even of the British empire. It is fighting to defend its soil, its history, its past, its future, its freedom, its civilization. We are .therefore fighting for a Christian ideal, for human civilization, for the liberty of the individual.
On what does victory depend? Only recently, a country's power was measured by its armed strength. To-day, in balancing the factors of strength, purely military might no longer has the absolute importance it once had. The strength of the best armed nation can only be measured in terms of its economic superiority. This is clearly shown by the methodical manner in which the enemy has used all his material and moral resources, as well as by the resistance offered by England, Czechoslovakia and Russia. The defeat of France is another evidence of that fact. Do you know how many German soldiers broke through the French line at Sedan, smashed the British and Belgian forces in Flanders, and destroyed at one fell swoop an army of five million Frenchmen? One hundred and fifty thousand men. Twelve panzer divisions with the assistance of a few thousand aeroplanes conquered France. The million German soldiers who followed had only a minor part to play: occupation.
Since war on the one hand brings into play all the strength and resources of the belligerent nations and since on the other hand the strength and resources of the warring countries will not become exhausted at the same time or in a single day, the basic problem in this war is one that implies a total as well as a lasting effort. Victory will come to whoever has sufficient resources to achieve a lasting effort, and enough strength to wear out the enemy.
The moral factor is an important part of that strength. In fact, public opinion or the morale of the people is an integral part of a nation's potential. History shows that an army which has a high morale and is fully conscious of its objective is a victorious army. To-day because of the constant risks of life modern man has become accustomed to calculation and reasoning, to appreciation of interdependent factors and to comparison of values. Man obeys a command and accepts a sacrifice for a purpose whenever he is in a position to appreciate the necessity of it.
Under what conditions is this long-drawn total effort to be carried on? Owing to the variety and multiplicity of needs, to the wide distribution of natural resources and to the highly specialized character of producticn, no one territory is capable of meeting alone the exigencies of a long-drawn-out war. Control of the sources of supply is essential to success. These sources are numerous, varied and scattered. Such control therefore implies freedom and mastery of the seas. The successful outcome of the war is therefore dependent upon a rational coordination of the total war effort contributed by each allied country.
A total effort, an enduring effort and a united determination to win, such are, Mr. Speaker, the conditions essential to victory.
In making its contribution each country will seek efficiency rather than quantity. Each country will take stock of the general need, of its own means and of the potential capacity of the Allied, Nations. Such contribution cannot be the same in each case, neither as to form, extent or kind.
These brief remarks may serve to determine how Canada can and should do its duty as a warring nation.
To provide for its own defence is its first duty. As a French economist once stated, Canada is a geographical paradox.
Although its boundary follows a parallel of latitude, nature has, on the contrary, by its mountain ranges, its climatic zones, its natural resource deposits divided the North American continent along meridians of longitude. Canada is the outcome of a free pact between provinces possessing each its own charac-

The Address-Mr. Eudes

teristics inhabited by ethnical groups of various origins, cultures and ideals. A deeper interest has served to unite them on a broader basis.
For the sake of security, the government must maintain these ethnical groups and dissimilar elements properly balanced and united. The existing bond must be strengthened and, in public policy, every step that might be of such a nature as to endanger harmonious relations or would not entirely promote the common good should be consistently avoided. In the interest of security, the government is also bound to provide for the defence of the country and all civil needs.
It is only after these civil needs are met, after the home defence is organized, in other words, after public security is assured, that Canada will be in a position to contribute to the allies' war effort. Otherwise the Canadian war effort would fall short of its object.
In order to reach maximum efficiency, our effort must take into account both our own possibilities and the needs of the allied nations. England, Russia, China, Australia and north Africa may all become theatres of war, and it is evident that this situation hampers the development of resources and the production of equipment and food in all these countries.
The considerable proportion of their population thus released from these various activities can without inconvenience be assigned to purely military tasks.
Because of its geographical situation, our country enjoys a greater measure of security than the other allied nations. Not that Canada is entirely safe from attack, but the geographical situation of the enemy countries as compared with its own makes it more secure. Consequently, Canadian production is less likely to suffer interruptions liable to jeopardize victory. On the other hand, Canada's natural resources are vast and varied. Its soil is fertile. Its population, however, is small, and this fact is aggravated by the dispersion of this population over a narrow stretch of land extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
In order to be logical and to attain its fullest effectiveness, Canada's contribution to the joint war effort must therefore be concentrated upon the production and the supply to the allied countries of the war material and foodstuffs which they cannot produce or can produce only in insufficient quantities. Anything that interferes with the accomplishment of this task is an obstacle to the role which Canada is expected to play in the defence of freedom and civilization.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that no one can honestly deny that Canada has so far
[Mr. Eudes.J
filled this role to the fullest. It must not be forgotten that when war was declared Canada had only recently emerged from a depression. Its agriculture and its manufacturing industry were just beginning to adapt themselves to the new markets they had had great difficulty in securing.
I invite those who criticize, either through inclination, interest or partisanship, to compare the quantity, quality and variety of our production, the effectives of our different armed forces, the amount of money raised by taxation and loans, in a word Canada's total contribution of to-day, with that of the last war. I ask them to think of the innumerable difficulties-the problems of transportation, to name only one of them

which this economic revolution, for that is what it really is, has involved. If they are sincere they will admit that our country has performed marvels. Our allies, the British people and their prime minister, our neighbours to the south and their president, have repeatedly praised and admired our achievement.
Yet, certain people are crying failure and demanding the head of the only man capable of carrying through the gigantic task which Canada has undertaken. Why? Because he has refused to yield to their wishes and make overseas military service compulsory.
In order to appraise it on its merits, conscription should be given its true perspective in the whole Canadian problem. This problem, I think I have shown, consists in providing collective security, in supplying our allies with foodstuffs and weapons, in maintaining an army, a navy and an air force. These four things are essential. Each one requires the same measure of attention in order that, a proper balance existing between them, the effort devoted to one of them may not injure the others. So, conscription is not an end in Canada's war effort. It is but a means of increasing the strength of the active army. Such is the only fair way of sizing up its importance.
Being a means, conscription must be judged by its results. If the latter are good, then conscription is desirable. If it impairs the efficiency of Canada's contribution to the common war effort, it must ruthlessly be rejected.
Let us now examine the effects of conscription. It will certainly be harmful to the war industry. It will take able-bodied men off the land, where they are already more and more needed. No one can deny the prime importance in this war of the navy and the air force, recruits for which are trained in this country. It is hard to see how conscrip-

The Address-Mr. Eudes
tion will help either of these .two services. On the contrary, it is liable to disorganize the navy and cripple the air training plan.
Moreover, the controversy that has developed about conscription shows that the latter has not the unanimous support of public opinion. Consequently, it is a serious threat to national unity. Besides, it is a coercive measure, and coercion destroys enthusiasm and heroism, without which no victory can be won.
And if Canada were attacked, does any one believe that the soldiers sent to England or Asia through conscription-a mere handful of men in the allied armies-could defend our territoiy?
I cannot understand, Mr. Speaker, the admonishments given to the French Canadians by certain persons who urge them to desist from opposing conscription. I think I have clearly shown that conscription is not a problem restricted to Quebec. It concerns the whole Canadian people. Besides,-as has been stated by many honourable members from different provinces-the French Canadians have identified themselves with the cause defended by Canada and her allies with the devotion, the bravery and1 the generosity characteristic of the French soul. It follows, Mr. Speaker, that under the circumstances conscription is a nefarious theory, hardly consistent with true partiotism.
To my mind, such is the material contribution of Canada to the war. Before discussing her moral contribution, I wish to say a few words about the plebiscite.
It has been claimed that the government should have continued to administer the public affairs without resorting to a plebiscite. I sincerely confess that I would have preferred such an attitude. However, I cannot be persuaded that a member elected1 by the people can oppose the plebiscite. A democratic government derives its mandate from the people. The latter are governed by their elected representatives, who in turn must express the views of their constituents in so far as they do not conflict with the common weal. It is claimed that former statements by government leaders gave no indication that a plebiscite would be held and that, consequently, parliament should reject such a measure.
Does such reasoning sufficiently take into account every element of the problem? Politics must ensure the common good within the limits set by justice, charity and liberty. How can politics hope to live up to such virtues when deliberately setting aside the needs of the hour for the consideration of
statements made under different circumstances and of directions designed to deal with needs which are no longer the same to-day.
Some still contend that the government cannot now break pledges taken at the time of the last general elections. Perfectly true. Does it follow that the parties to such contract are incapable of modifying its terms by common consent? Now, in a plebiscite, the government is asking the people if they believe that a clause in that contract between them should be changed. Should the people refuse, then such clause would remain in its original form. To refuse a contracting party the right of consulting the other is the very denial of liberty. To refuse the right of holding a plebiscite is to deny to the people the exercise of an inherent privilege of liberty, that of stating one's opinion, a privilege which the democratic system does essentially grant to the people.
In order that their war contribution may be thoroughly efficient, the Canadian people must be united in their ardent and enthusiastic determination to win. A lofty conception of their purpose must serve as the inspiration for the necessary sacrifices they must accept.
Why is there war? Why this tremendous sacrifice of the Canadian people? Is it simply for the joy of victory, simply to preserve prewar conditions under which the individual certainly did not enjoy the fair share of well-being which the state should provide? No. We are not fighting for victory alone, but for peace, for real peace. And this does not mean the mere absence of conflict. It means a state wherein, under the aegis of justice, charity and liberty, human faculties may attain a full development. Post-war will be such as we shall have made it. The people have selected us to direct their destinies. A politician must not let events overtake him. He must scan the future that he may foresee and master it.
The new order which the post-war period will bring cannot easily be foreseen in every detail. It must first be born in the heart of each and every one. Then only can the state supply the appropriate setting wherein legitimate needs may obtain just satisfaction. Democracy will supply this setting. For the democratic formula is not static. It is dynamic and naturally tends towards improvement.
Our government has already taken steps in this direction. Under the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) a group of experts are studying post-war problems. On the other hand, unemployment insurance, stabilized trade and prices and other measures al-e due to temper the trying hours of the post-war days to come.
The Address-Mr. Eudes

These measures are but the first step. Dealing with one of its aspects only is not solving the whole problem. The inauguration of a new order presupposes a general consideration of all post-war problems and a thorough knowledge of all questions relating to manpower and material.
This new order must be founded on justice and freedom. But there can be no justice unless the rights of the poor, the workers, the minorities and every other class are respected. Without equality and fraternity, justice is a vain word. However, equality and fraternity lose their beneficial character when the leaders use them as a bait for the weak and the lowly.
Liberty must be enjoyed by everyone. Enjoyment of power, privileges and fortune by a few while the majority labour under the weight of restraint cannot be considered as freedom. There is no freedom in the absence of political rights and these are a , mere illusion unless accompanied by economic rights. There is no freedom for the worker whose future is unsettled. Finally no freedom is possible unless the representatives of the people govern with the greatest possible efficiency.
Mr. Speaker, this new order erected on justice and freedom is our goal. I am confident that our efforts will not be in vain, which would be the case unless we are guided by the principles for which we are fighting. In the present conflict we fight the enemy by our own methods. It were better not to fight than to use nazi methods.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I express the hope that when the struggle is ended in victory, this new order will prevail. Let us spread this ideal through the land. Let everyone's ambition be that of living in a united Canada in the enjoyment of justice and freedom. Then will our efforts and our hearts be united through the struggle ended by victory, for if it be true that men die in combat, it is equally true that nations often disappear for refusing to fight.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few observations on the question now before the house, may I grasp this belated opportunity to congratulate the hon. gentlemen who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I should like to compliment them upon the splendid speeches which they made in moving and seconding that motion. I venture to say, and I believe most hon. members will agree, that the material which they used in their
[Mr. Eudes.)
presentations.was excellent; and I believe that if we turned back over the pages of Hansard we should find that their speeches have been excelled by few.
The hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier) and the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) had the splendid opportunity of visiting England and seeing conditions there at first hand. They naturally, therefore, speak with some authority. They have returned to Canada and have given us a vivid picture of what those stout-hearted people of Britain are enduring in this tremendous conflict.
In passing, I should like to compliment the hon. member for Northumberland, N.B. (Mr. O'Brien), who a few evenings ago gave us of this house an opportunity of seeing some of the pictures which he had taken in England, and of realizing more fully the courage and endurance of those brave people. I have personally spoken to a number of Canadians who recently returned from Britain, and have been amazed at what I have learne'd of the gallantry and determination of the British people, and the sacrifices which they are making to preserve freedom not only for themselves but for all the peoples of the world.
I recall a speech made in this house by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) on November 19, 1940, reported on page 208 of Hansard. He said:
Some two months ago I listened^ to a radio commentator from London who said that one of the amazing sights in that great city, was the number of flags that could be seen flying there. Most touching of all, I thought, was his statement that in instance after instance these flags could be seen floating over ruined buildings, many of them the humble dwellings of the poor. These people, forced to see their homes destroyed, their personal possessions gone, sometimes members of their families maimed or killed, digged themselves out of the wreckage and at once they planted above it the flag of Britain. That act seems to me symbolic. They plant that great flag there, not only to defy Hitler, not only to encourage the weak and ' inspire the faltering among themselves, but also as an emblem of hope and of prophecy. And the hope and the prophecy are this: that just as the flag of Britain rises over the physical ruins of some of its homes, so out of the wreck and welter of this war there will arise a greater Britain, a Britain strengthened and stiffened by its heroic struggle, a Britain which will lead the world into better and fairer ways of life, not for one class or group, but for all people.
So long as that spirit remains we need have no doubt as to the ultimate outcome of this war. The whole of Britain is under attack now, but in her own time she and her dominions will take the offensive. They are on the offensive even now; for our gallant airmen are carrying the war to the heart of enemy countries and to the territories which Germany has conquered,

The Address-Mr. Rennie
and our incomparable fleet still commands the seas. Her soldiers at Dunkirk have proven their quality We shall see Britain triumphant, anci long after the name of Hitler will have become nothing but an unpleasant memory, the same flag which now waves over disordered heaps of crumbled brick and stone and mortar will be flying freely and proudly in the airs of heaven, sheltering liberty and justice and freedom and truth in its benevolent shade. That is the hope and the promise of the British flag flying over the ruins of British homes.
In these difficult days, when our empire is faced with the greatest crisis in its history, one cannot help but recall the words of a great Canadian, Doctor MacDonald, when he said on one occasion, "It would be indeed a calamity beyond compare were that world empire broken and its fragments scattered abroad." Yet on the other side of the picture one has the encouraging words of Burke, who said that the ties of empire are as light as air but strong as links of steel.
In the preservation of this British empire we need to-day the encouraging words of Burke. Canadians played a great part in the first world war, and when the history of that war was written the pages were bright with the matchless deeds of valour of our men. And, sir, after a quarter of a century we still think of those fine, stout-hearted men and their deeds at Ypres, Passchendaele, the Somme and Vimy Ridge. So to-day we must show to the world that what Canada did in 1914-18, Canada can do to-day on a larger scale.
But in order that we shall do our best in this country there must be cooperation on the part of every individual citizen of this dominion. Cooperation is not merely a sentiment; it is an economic necessity. The efforts of every man and woman in this dominion I believe should be directed through the government into the avenues of service for which they find themselves best fitted. May I quote here Mr. Churchill's words spoken in this chamber on December 30, 1941, as reported at page 4480 of Hansard, January 21, 1942:
In this strange, terrible world war there is a place for everyone, man and woman, old and young, hale and halt. Service in a thousand forms is open. There is no room now for the dilettante, for the weakling, for the shirker or the sluggard. The mine, the factory, the dockyard, the salt sea waves, the fields to till, the home, the hospital, the chair of the scientist, the pulpit of the preacher-from the highest to the humblest, the tasks are all of equal honour. All have their part to play. [DOT]
I think it is the consensus of the Canadian people that Canada has taken a preeminent position in this great world scene. Men have their own views on politics and on political personalities; they may prefer one Canadian statesman to another. These are important
matters; they are the blood and bone and muscle of democracy at work. But in a world convulsed with the mighty shock of the fiercest war of which history has record, factional, political and partisan differences should sink into their proper and proportionate place. When great forces are in action, with powerful tides and undercurrents sweeping over and through countries and peoples, the obvious has a way of being overlooked. But just because a fact is obvious it is not less significant. It is no less fraught with rich cargoes of ideas and ideals. Obviously Winston Churchill is the man of the hour of Britain; obviously President Roosevelt is the man of the hour in the United States; obviously Joseph Stalin is the man of the hour in Russia, and obviously Prime Minister Mackenzie King is the man of the hour in Canada.
While there are some who are outspoken in their condemnation of the Prime Minister's policy for Canada's war effort, these same critics are just as ready to admit that because of the happy personal relations between the Prime Minister of Canada and the President of the United States, relationships which have their roots in the common understanding of the ways of life of Canada and the United States, the three thousand miles of unfortified border between the two countries are marked with the personalities of Mackenzie King and Roosevelt. Who but our Prime Minister could have appealed to the United States in forthright language for help for Great Britain? Our Prime Minister did this in a broadcast from London last year. Canada could speak to the United States as an American nation.
Did not Canada declare war on Germany of her own volition? And in the succeeding year under the good neighbour policy our Prime Minister entered into a joint north American agreement with President Roosevelt. When Pearl Harbour was attacked, Canada declared war on Japan in advance of both the United States and Great Britain. Canada could do these things because, to put it bluntly, she was a free agent. Canada is a member of the British commonwealth of nations, but she is a nation. She showed her loyalty to the crown in the brilliant reception given to Their Majesties King George and Queen Elizabeth in 1939. She again showed , her loyalty in the tumultuous welcome given to Winston Churchill in Ottawa. So I say, how properly can we assay the qualities, the seemingly paradoxical qualities of Canada? With the structure of the world organization rudely, roughly shaken, Canada, through her Prime Minister, became the stabilizer and acted to maintain the equilibrium. Winston
The Address-Mr. Rennie

Churchill perfectly illustrates the situation. He visits Washington; he comes to Ottawa, and then' visits Washington again. Speaking in this very chamber Prime Minister Churchill said:
Canada, sir, occupies a unique position in the British empire because of its unbreakable ties with Britain and its ever-growing friendship and intimate association with the United States. Canada is a potent magnet, drawing together those in the new world and in the old whose fortunes are now united in a deadly struggle for life and honour against the common foe.
I should like to say a word on behalf of that great mass of patriotic men and women in Canada who derive their living from tilling the soil. In my own county, according to the latest available figures, we have a land area of about 489,000 acres; the number of occupied farms is about 5,000, and the farm population is something over 20,467. These fine men and women are bending every effort to help Canada fill her quotas of cheese, bacon, eggs and other farm products for Britain, and in order to do this they are toiling from early morning until late at night. There is no eight-hour day for these hard-working people. I should like to quote a few words from the very fine address of the Prime Minister on January 26, when he presented to this parliament what one might call Canada's balanced war effort. He said, at page 34 of Hansard:
A vital aspect of Canada's war effort is our contribution to the food supply of Great Britain. This contribution has grown steadily in importance. Britain cannot feed herself, and her own great and growing armed forces. Still less can she feed the ever-increasing numbers of men we are sending from Canada to add to her armed strength. In the present war, unlike the last, her sources of food on the continent of Europe have all been closed off by enemy occupation. Canada is the nearest source of food left open. Without our food, the people of Britain might starve.
Then, at page 40 of Hansard, the Prime Minister went on to say:
Canada has contracts with Great Britain for bacon, hams and other pork products amounting to 618,000,000 pounds. The forthcoming agreement for cheese is expected to be for at least 125,000,000 pounds. Then, 675,000 cases of evaporated milk will probably, again this year, be required by Britain. The present contract for eggs is for 30,000,000 dozen. Further large contracts for summer and fall delivery are anticipated. Canada has also undertaken to supply Britain with 4,500,000 pounds of honey; 510,000 barrels of fresh apples; 425,000 cases of processed apples; 300,000 cases of canned tomatoes, and other fruit and vegetable products in substantial quantities. Altogether, the value of the exports of the above commodities will be at least
8180.000.	000. Exports of the same products in the year before the war were valued at about
850.000.	000.
TMr. Rennie.]
Prosperity on the land, Mr. Speaker, means prosperity for all. I believe no calling surpasses farming from the standpoint of health and vigour, both of body and of intellect. Farmers as a class do not ask for charity; they are willing to work for what they get. Moreover, they constitute such a large proportion of our population that their welfare demands the consideration of all. This, coupled with the fact that they are engaged in our basic industry, makes the need for such consideration doubly great. Unfortunately many city people do not know the farmer. They have no appreciation of what he contributes to Canadian life as a whole, or the relationship that exists between his work and the earning of a livelihood in urban centres. So that in passing I should like to mention briefly one or two points which I believe are in the interests of the farmer, because after all I believe farming holds the key to prosperity in Canada and that this basic industry must therefore come first in legislative thought and action.
I should like to touch briefly on the mobilization act, in regard to young men being called up for training. I come from military district No. 1, which has contributed a great many fine young men both for overseas service and for the defence of Canada. But I have long since come to the conclusion that it is most unreasonable that we in Canada should take away from our farms the help that is so essential if we are to produce the food supplies which the Prime Minister stressed so much in his address a few days ago. I appreciate the fact that if a young man appeals to the registrar he is given consideration. In passing I should like to express my appreciation of the work done by Mr. Martin, registrar for military district No. 1. I do not know the gentleman very well; I have never gone to him to ask that any young man be relieved from training, but I believe he is a reasonable and fair-minded man, who gives every consideration to any request he receives, which is as it should be. The point I should like to make, however, and the point I should like to draw to the attention of the government, is this. I do not believe that in this crisis, when the farmers are finding things most difficult, they should have postponements for only perhaps six months. A young man who is on a farm, where the only other available labour is that of an old man perhaps fifty or sixty or seventy years of age, should be given an undertaking that he will not be called for military service, because I do not believe any industry requires early preparation for its annual activities more than does farming. Then, too-and this is not a new thought-we realize that the farmer

The Address-Mr. Rennie
is greatly handicapped in having to pay wages more or less equivalent to those paid in factories making the munitions of war.
I have every confidence in our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and I believe the policies w'hich will be worked out by the government for this year will be of benefit to the farmer. But I suggest to the minister that these policies should not be left in abeyance any longer. Let us frame our programme so that the farmer will know this spring just what his position will be, so that he may put in his seed as early as possible.
There is another point in connection with farming I should like to mention in passing. I refer to the price of farm implements. I realize, too, that in war-time farm implements are bound to cost more money. Nevertheless I believe some arrangement should be made by the government under which the prices of what the farmer has to buy will be closer to parity with the prices of the commodities he offers for sale.
I come from a part of Canada in which the growing of tobacco has developed into a great industry. I would ask the government to realize that this is a seasonal occupation. The men involved have spent large sums of money in equipping their farms. Usually they have five or six kilns costing about $500 each. I am inclined to the belief that in connection with the sale of tobacco there is something radically wrong with the process of grading. I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to give the matter his attention.
May I be permitted to say a few words respecting compulsory service, and the committee for total war. I shall state frankly that I have taken exception to that committee for calling men from ail parts of Ontario to attend a dinner at the Royal York hotel, without first informing those men as to the matters to be discussed at the meeting. I know some men attended the meeting believing it to be called for the purpose of organizing the victory loan campaign, and they were somewhat disappointed when they learned otherwise. In my view the committee by its agitation did more harm than good. Had their method been one of cooperation rather than one of destroying and tearing down, they would have contributed much more to Canada's war effort.
Although I have not the authority for this, I am told that the cost of advertising and other activities of the committee must have been somewhere in the neighbourhood of $150,000 to $200,000. In addition to that, large quantities of gasoline were used by two hundred men who drove to Toronto from all parts of Ontario. Had the committee put that amount of money to the credit of the government to purchase a corvette or a minesweeper, or some equipment for the benefit of our soldiers, it would have been making a greater contribution.
I received letters and cards from my own constituency, some of which were in favour of a total war effort, some in favour of conscription of man-power only, and some in favour of conscription of wealth. But from a constituency with a voting'population of about
35,000,	in comparison the number of letters and cards received was small.
In my constituency the committee for total war, sincere in its efforts but overzealous in its patriotism and its wish to see the war ended as soon as possible, gave vent to its feelings through the medium of this organization. I have received telegrams from my constituency, some of which favoured, and others of which objected to the operations of that committee. For instance, I hold in my hand a letter from a veteran of the last war, an extract from which I shall read to the house:
As a veteran of the last war, I suppose I might be expected to be in full support of a total war effort. This is so true that I ani prepared to place my property at the disposal of the government, and serve in any capacity at the army scale of pay, if the people behind this movement, including those who signed the petition, are prepared to do the same. But I am not prepared to assist in any way to conscript my neighbor's son on any other basis. You probably know that at least some of the people whose names appeared as taking the petition, made fortunes out of the last war and hope to add to them out of this one; and I want to record my objection as strongly as possible to this conscription for the other fellow. I have no authority to speak for others, but I am sure you would find my sentiments approved by a large majority of people, irrespective of politics.
And one other clipping:
I have three sons in the air force, and I applied for enlistment myself. I do not know about military conscription. If it were absolutely necessary, I suppose it will have to be; but I believe a good, honest, wholehearted war effort, governed by good sense as at present, is what I stand for.
I should like now to touch on the question of the bits-and-pieces programme which has been functioning under the Department of Munitions and Supply. In that connection I would register a complaint which, I believe, is worthy of consideration and is in fact receiving some consideration. I am inclined to the belief that in this great war effort, and especially in connection with the development of our industry, there has been too much centralization in the larger centres, with the result that the smaller towns have not had the opportunity to compete in connection with a variety of industrial activities.

The Address-Mr. Rennie
There are many small towns in Ontario where the housing situation is not acute, and where large numbers of men could be accommodated1. But we find that at least up to the present time industry has been directed toward the larger cities. I leave this thought with the. government, in the hope that as time passes this condition may be remedied.
I should like to make a few brief observations concerning the plebiscite. I did not feel I could add much to the debate, but I do wish to make my position perfectly clear in regard to this important matter. When I had the honour of being elected as member for the constituency of Oxford, I believed that in all matters of public interest I should use my best judgment in respect of any action I might take. I believed that that should be my course with respect to matters such as the one I am now discussing. Having first obtained information as to the facts, I believed I should vote according to the dictates of my own conscience, and, Mr. Speaker, that is what I intend to do. I believe in the truth of the old adage that honesty is the best policy. The Prime Minister and practically every hon. member supporting the government stated clearly during the 1940 election campaign, "No conscription of men for overseas service." Doctor Manion, the then leader of the National Conservative party, also made his position clear. Some have urged that because the government has the largest number of supporters, it should disregard its pledge. My thought is that the larger numbers on the government side constitute all the more reason why they should appeal to the people and have the people make the decision.
At the moment I am not saying what stand I should take if it comes to a matter of conscription. I reserve that decision for myself. In the light of my vote on the plebiscite -and I shall vote for the plebiscite-I shall then endeavour to gather a knowledge of the facts, as I have done in this instance, and shall try to vote intelligently on the matter of conscription when it becomes an issue.
At this point I had intended to quote some authorities to support my vote on the plebiscite. I had intended to quote the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), than whom there is no more outstanding man in this great dominion. I refer hon. members to his speech. In this connection I think of the Prime Minister's speech with respect to the plebiscite. I think, too, of the fine contribution made to the debate by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). I think of the splendid contributions of the Minister
[Mr. Rennie.l
of National Defence, (Mr. Ralston) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I have perfect confidence in these men who are trying to direct Canada's war effort, and while I am in this house I shall be guided considerably by them. I feel that after all they know the situation better than we do; and more than anything else I am interested in the preservation of the unity of this great dominion of Canada. National unity is no bogy. National unity is of vital importance, even beyond the present crisis. After this war we shall have to face tremendous problems of world reconstruction and nations and men of goodwill must cooperate. I believe that Kipling's "The Law of the Jungle" still holds good:
For the strength of the pack is the wolf,
and the strength of the wolf is the pack.
How can we play a part in the new world order if we have failed in the duties of brotherhood and cooperation here in our own country? With tolerance and goodwill at home we shall have taken a long step toward helping in an international world and toward the solution of Canada's own social and economic problems. Canadian unity, warm, effective and vital, is the key to our entire future.
During the last war I think all men in Canada had great admiration for Marshal Foch who led the allied armies. He represented to us the type of perfectly functioning mind which amid the storms and stresses of conflict found its way to victory. I recall that on one occasion when General Foch was addressing the students of the war college in France he said:
You are to be the brains of an army, I beseech you in the name of God, think!
In so many places tolerance and friendship have been replaced by bitterness, freedom has given way to tyranny, the light of democracy has been somewhat extinguished. I can think of no more needed message to leave with the leaders of this country than words similar to those Marshal Foch uttered to the men who were to lead the armies of France:
You are to be leaders in the nation;
You are the builders of Canada;
You are thinking for the people,
I beseech you in the name of God, think!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question now before the house has been under debate for over three weeks, so I appreciate fully that anything I may say will be largely repetition. But I feel that I cannot let the question pass without making a few suggestions, and I shall try to be brief in my remarks. It seems a peculiar state of affairs, and there must be something

The Address-Mr. MdcKenzie (Lambton)
radically wrong with world conditions, that after engaging in and winning a world war in 1914-18, and after dictating the terms of peace, in a little over twenty years we should be in a second world war which is being waged with much greater fury, more powerful armaments and equipment, and with much more disastrous results to both human life and property than the war of 1914-18. Winning this war is essential, but winning the peace that will be a lasting peace, that will give us national security, is much more important.
We are facing the greatest crisis, not only of this century but in the world's history. So much has been said about total war effort and total mobilization of all our resources that the average Canadian citizen is confused as to what total war means and what is really needed for a total war effort. Every Canadian worthy of the name wants this to be a total war. I shall not repeat in this house details of the magnificent contribution Canada has made thus far in the war with her air force, her navy, her army and the great industrial development that has taken place in providing munitions and instruments of war, when, prior to September, 1939, practically all of Canada's industries were engaged in supplying domestic needs. In the present situation the drive for total war and conscription was made by a powerful Toronto group backed by an extensive newspaper campaign. This question of total war first arose in Toronto, then in Montreal, and then it spread throughout Canada and has caused a great deal of confusion. If it can be proved or successfully argued that the previous pledge not to conscript men for overseas service without consulting the people has actually impaired the war effort thus far; if there is a serious shortage of enlistments to fill out the plans of the army chiefs; if there is any shortage of industrial man-power to turn out the instruments of war, then the issue would be much clearer. But the best sources of information in Ottawa state that none of these things are true. However, the time may come when that will not be so and, of course, we must be prepared.
One of the greatest dangers to an all-out war effort is, I believe, a shortage of labour on the farm. I am speaking now particularly of Ontario where many hired men have left the farms to work in munitions plants for wages the farmer cannot afford to pay. In many cases the farm boy was drafted for military training, and when he asked for postponement he was, in some cases, advised by the Department of National War Services to take his four months' training in the winter' when farm work is slack so that he might be home for 44561-42
seeding and harvesting. The act was, however, changed, and these boys now find themselves in the army for the duration of the war with very little hope of getting released. I believe it would be in the national interest if all farmers who are in the armed forces and who are needed on the farms were given leave of absence for seeding and harvesting. If this is not done, I fear our farmers will not be able to supply the foodstuffs that may be required for the feeding of Britain and our allies.
I shall place the contributing forces in three categories, and one is probably just as important as the other: the armed forces, the instruments of war and munitions, and the supplying of foodstuffs. The latter could easily be the deciding factor in the ultimate conclusion of the war. I have received many postcards from residents in my riding, and no doubt many hon. members have had a similar experience, which read:
I believe the most efficient and honourable way for Canada to prosecute total war is by compulsory selective service without restrictions. The government of Canada should introduce this measure so that men who are best on the farms will be placed on the farms; those who are most helpful in the factories will work in the factories, and those best fitted will serve in the armed forces, wherever needed. Such a plan is fair to all the people of Canada.
That, would be conscription of man-power, but would it be an all-out effort? We all remember back in 1914-18 when many thousands of Canadian soldiers went to Europe to fight, many paying the supreme sacrifice. But what happened at home? At that time many industries made so much money because of the war, that they have never had to do much since-many millions were made. At the beginning of this war the government took the stand that a similar situation must not exist, and the Excess Profits Tax Act was passed. This would take by taxation over eighty per cent of all profits made in excess of the profits made in the average four years preceding 1939. There was some logic in this because of the experience of the last war, but it does not go far enough. Many industries made big dividends during the four years prior to 1939, and they should be required to make an equal contribution. War at the best is waste. What financier, what farmer, what employee, what man in the armed forces should hope to come out of this war as well off financially as when he went into it? Nevertheless, many thousands of people apparently do. We talk about equality of service and sacrifice; how much has the average man in Canada sacrificed? If total war means contribution in kind and according to ability to winning the war, then total war

The Address-Mr. MacKenzie (Lambton)
must reach everyone, no matter who he or she may be. It must exempt no one. Then, if you divide the contributing forces into the three categories, the armed forces, the factories, and the farm, they should be put as nearly as possible on the same pay basis.
The income tax does take a large toll on salaries and on the revenue that is derived from our investments, but it does not go far enough. If the government is going to organize labour completely, it must also organize and regiment the capital resources of this nation. The Toronto Globe and Mail a few days ago in an editorial claimed that some people, when talking about conscription of wealth, meant confiscation of wealth. I do not think that is anyone's intention or is in anyone's mind. But what if some wealth had to be confiscated? What happens to the young man who gives his all, his life? Is that not confiscation? What about the soldier who comes back from the war crippled and broken in health? Is his health not confiscated? We say that the government looks after him and his dependents, and the Canadian government has done as well as or better than most other countries in looking after our war veterans; yet I know of several men who served in the last war who, because the pension board does not attribute their disabilities to war causes, are deprived of a pension or have to eke out an existence on a war veteran's allowance. We talk glibly about an all-out war effort, but let us go all the way. We live in a democracy; then let us start with the highest office in the dominion and end with the private in the army or the labouring man and be as nearly equal in service and sacrifice as possible until this war is won.
We have in Canada a fairly large population of foreign birth. Many have taken out their citizenship papers, and are good loyal Canadian citizens. Under the provisions of our Naturalization Act they must be domiciled within the British empire for five years before they can become naturalized citizens. Many find themselves in an embarrassing position because they have not been here for five years. I submit that the Naturalization Act should be amended so that they can take out their first or second year citizenship papers and assume their responsibilities as such, or else the mobilization act should be amended so that they, too, can contribute towards our war effort-and many of them are anxious to do their share.
We have many non-permanent reserve units in Canada, and I doubt if they are making any worth-while contribution to our war effort. There may have been a time in the

early days of the war when they served a useful purpose, but with the selective drafts now in operation they are not much support to recruiting. I am not able to find out the exact number of these units, but there are probably eighty or ninety units of infantry, and probably nearly as many artillery units. Each unit has from two to four fulltime officers, with the rank of anywhere from corporal to lieutenant-colonel. They usually train part-time a couple of nights a week. I contend that they are an added expense and are not making any werth-while contribution, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these units should be mobilized for active service either at home or abroad, or dispensed with altogether. The defence department has worked out something along this line but it does not go far enough.
In 1867 the fathers of confederation were successful in uniting the two great races of this continent, with the status of equal rights and privileges, and with a common purpose for a united Canada. After seventy-five years have we been successful, and if not, why not? We have gone a long way, it is true, but I should like to see a law passed that would make it a serious offence for any politician to raise a racial or a religious cry in order to gain some political advantage. We must admit that that has been done many times in the past, and no true patriot would do it.
My father came to Canada as a young immigrant boy from Scotland. My mother's ancestors also came from Scotland and I have a great regard for the mother country. True, I am a Canadian first, but I believe that Canada will give her all to aid the motherland at, this time.
Unfortunately politics has apparently entered into this question, and the question of conscription cannot be fairly dealt with on that basis. I stated in my election campaign of 1940 that I was opposed to conscription and did not believe it was necessary, and that the voluntary system was the best. I am still opposed to the principle of conscription; it is foreign to the very spirit of democracy. In this present crisis, if conscription is necessary to win this war, let us not only conscript man-power but go all the way and conscript all our resources. We already have conscription, and it is selective so far as age groups and medical fitness go. Young men are being conscripted every day for the army, and conscripted for the duration of the war.
We have three Ministers of National Defence. We have faith in these men. They have surrounded themselves with qualified military men and army advisers, and these

The Address-Mr. Roy
military authorities in cooperation with the British war office should know where these troops can best meet the enemy and engage them. If outside Canada, so much the better. If we expect help in case of attack or invasion, and we might need it, surely we must be prepared to give help. Look at the map of the world in September, 1939, and look at it to-day; and then ask yourself, are we winning this war?
The plebiscite will not settle this question of conscription for the armed forces overseas. It was never intended that it should. If that question is introduced by the government, it will be settled on the floor of this house and members will make their own decision in view of all the Circumstances, and abide by the consequences. I have faith that, if properly presented, the plebiscite will carry, and if we must have a plebiscite, let us bring in the bill without delay and get it over with. Anything that tends to confuse, retards our war effort. I cannot see why objection to the plebiscite should be regarded as a want-of-confidence motion. I do not consider it as such. We are living in the darkest days of Canadian history and we have a job to do. Let not politics or anything else interfere with it. Let us get on with the job.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fain would express the usual commendations in connection with the speech from the throne and compliment the mover of the address (Mr. Fournier), as well as the seconder (Mr. Macdonald, Brantford), without excepting the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), but the measures announced and the statements contained in the speeches are of such a distressing nature as to Leave me no inclination to compliment their authors. Congratulations are worthless unless sincere. The remarks I desire to make are far from congratulatory. You may be positive that I deeply deplore this fact.
Besides various financial measures of an astonishing character, the speech from the throne announces a plebiscite to release the government from pledges and commitments concerning conscription and to allow them to alter the methods of raising men for service overseas. In fact, this is the last step towards conscription as the Prime Minister told us in his speech of January 26, as reported on page 44 of Hansard:
National selective service is the method by which the government proposes to accomplish the mobilization of man-power on an extended scale. Let me define national service as it is understood by the government. By national service is meant any form of service, either voluntary or compulsory, which contributes directly to Canada's war effort.
And, later, he added:
In announcing that national selective service is the method by which the government proposes to accomplish the mobilization of man-power on an extended scale, the government is not announcing a new policy. What we propose to do is to extend what, in fact, we have been doing right along, that is, to apply the principle progressively. In other words, we intend to continue to extend the application of national selective service to meet new needs as they arise.
As I have already said, this policy, too, is not new, nor is it being advanced to-day for the first time, or as a consequence of high-pressure methods employed to influence the independence of members of parliament. The principle itself, as I have already explained, was approved by this parliament in June, 1940. It has already been applied to some extent. On November 12 last, I made it very plain to parliament that, with respect to the mobilization of man-power, the government's policy was one of national selective service; and, also, that an extension of the application of compulsory selective service-conscription, if you will-was a part of that policy.
Therefore, the Liberal party forgoes the doctrine which has ensured it public support for the last 25 years. This is a national political event the extreme importance of which no one underestimates.
The speech from the throne is a typical example of the usual methods used by the government in the consideration of a difficult problem and in the handling of a given situation. They wish to skirt the obstacle. So clever are they in their impertinence that they even attempt to bring the public to approve a policy that the Liberals have always represented as a national crime. The great question of the day is conscription for service anywhere in the world.
The Conservatives make it the main issue. An important number of English-speaking Liberal members are in favour of this measure. It is said that some members of the cabinet- and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) left little doubt on this subject in the minds of his hearers the other day-are conscriptionists at heart. The Prime Minister, a modern sphynx-and I regret his absence-claims that the government are gradually enforcing this measure; however, at the same time, he leaves us under the impression that he is opposed to it. He courts both the conscriptionists and the anti-conscriptionists. He claims that, in his mind, national unity is first and foremost.
In 1916 and 1917, did the Liberals act this way, did they give a thought to national unity? Have they preached a doctrine of unity, since then, while they were encouraging anti-conscriptionists in one part of the country and ultra-loyalists in another? Is it not to be feared that, at a time when national
The Address-Mr. Roy

unity ,is more necessary than ever, the impression may be gained that the chief purpose of the Prime Minister is to avoid a cabinet crisis and to preserve above all unity within the Liberal party.
Notwithstanding the complete reversal of their attitude the Liberal government make a show of fulfilling their promises. They assume an appearance of righteousness. They pretend to attach more importance to the pledged word. However, their opportunism causes them to create a political situation more and more tense and confused.
There are attitudes and statements that would be comical were they not so tragic.
The mover of the address, in expounding the policies of the government to the satisfaction of the Prime Minister has stated with a courage worthy of recognition, that he will ask his electors and his fellow-citizens to release the government from their promises and commitments against conscription and to accept the sacrifice of submitting to compulsory military services overseas, in order to preserve national unity.
At the outset of his remarks in reply to the speech delivered by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) on January 26, the Prime Minister blamed the Conservative leader for not having dared to use the word "conscription" in his amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, in spite of his advocacy of conscription in his speech.
The Prime Minister's outburst is all the more frivolous and childish that the said amendment provides for compulsory military service in all theatres of war. Moreover, when asked what he will do after the plebiscite will have released him from his pledges and his promises against conscription, the Prime Minister evaded the issue and refused to commit himself, though his intentions had been clearly -disclosed in the speech from the throne, in the speech of the hon. member who moved the address and in his own speech. It is a case of a mote in the neighbour's eye and a beam in one's own. The Prime Minister plays on words and obtains an easy victory.
After pointing out the gigantic proportions of our war effort and of our assistance and gifts to England, the Prime Minister declared that, except for some slight differences, the Liberal government's policy is the same as that of the Tory party in the matter of war and selective service. '
What an astonishing confession! The Prime Minister was certainly not thinking at the moment of all the abuse, opprobrium and ignominy the Liberal party had heaped on
[Vjr. Roy.]
this same Tory policy which it now makes its own. It must then be true that the punishment is found in the sin itself.
A little further on, perhaps under pangs of remorse, the Prime Minister candidly admits that, were it not for the pledges taken and the promises made during the provincial election campaign in 1939, the election results might perhaps have not been the same.
If it be true, Mr. Speaker, that inconsiderate pledges and promises were instrumental in tricking the people into approval in 1939, then the party led by the Prime Minister must also admit having as stealthily garnered the votes which returned them to power since 1921, for such is the only method they have used in every campaign. Is it to be wondered that rancours still endure and that bitter opposition is encountered? Neither should we wonder if, based on such methods, on prejudices and a most cynical opportunism, the government is now in a tottering situation and national unity is crumbling.
That very illusive national unity, invented for use by the Liberal party, based on nonparticipation in foreign wars and on insults for the opponents of this doctrine, is not the Prime Minister betraying it when, admitting that his party's successes are due to solemn pledges, he singles out as a target for prejudice that very province of Quebec which bore him to power and kept him there and which received at his hands that very political training which is now held against it? This is what the Prime Minister stated on January 26, as appears on page 46 of Hansard:
Hon. members are also aware that if, at the time when Canada's participation in the war was challenged in an election in the province of Quebec by a government professing a different political faith, a like assurance with respect to service overseas had not been given in the name of the present government by the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, by the Minister of Public Works (Mr Cardin), and other Liberal leaders and members of this House of Commons from the province of Quebec, the verdict of the people of that province might have been wholly different.
The Quebec Liberal leaders bear a great share of responsibility for the present situation and their electors [DOT]null certainly not be satisfied with fictitious and futile explanations nor with pious regrets. They will insist that these leaders protect them against conscription, as they agreed to do when they claimed to constitute their rampart against conscription. But wrhy does the Prime Minister, when mentioning those who have taken pledges and made commitments against conscription, always exclude himself and the English-speaking Liberal leaders?

The Address-Mr. Roy
Has not the Prime Minister himself spoken against conscription in his radio address to the nation at the beginning of the 1940 campaign? Has not the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated at Markineh, during that same campaign, that the Liberal government would never enforce conscription of manpower for overseas service? Again recently did not the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) go to Montreal in early December of 1941 and advocate opposition to this measure in the province of Quebec? Did not the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) also repeat recently his opposition to this measure which he called nefarious and futile. Has not the Prime Minister himself endorsed not only commitments against conscription but also promises made against any participation in empire wars by the then Minister of Justice, by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) and the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), when he wired Mr. Francoeur on December 26th, 1937, the following:
Lotbiniere electors have voted as Canadians who put national interest above all else.
I could submit evidence to the fact that English-Canadian Liberals, with the Prime Minister at their head, have just like French-Canadian Liberals advocated in this country, particularly in the Province of Quebec, a policy of non-participation to foreign wars and, right up to recent weeks, given solemn pledges against conscription. The country must surely be aware that they are all equally responsible in trying to win over public confidence by making false promises, as the Prime Minister admits.
Why are the Quebec Liberal leaders, the honourable Minister of Public Works and his friend, the late Mr. Lapointe, alone called upon by the Prime Minister to justify their stand before imperialistic opinion? The Prime Minister makes it necessary for us to denounce his ingratitude for those and for him to whom he owes his present position and all the honours conferred upon him; he would have us believe that his friendship for the late Mr. Lapointe, his friend and benefactor, was as artificial as the tribute to his memory paid by him in this house on January 21st last.

speechtext: What shameful language!
