speechtext:
It is a fact. To such evident proof of opportunism and lack of sincerity on the part of the Liberal party, I would add further evidence, more concrete proof, if I may so express myself. Let us look up page 363 of the Parliamentary Guide, Mr. Speaker, where the numerical strength of the various parties is mentioned. We see that in 1921,
out of 117 Liberal members, Quebec had contributed 65 to the Liberal party. In 1925, 60 out of 101; in 1926, 60 out of 116; in 1930, 40 out of 88. Up to that time, then, Quebec constituted the main element in the Liberal forces. But in the 1935 elections, we note that the other provinces swelled the ranks of the Liberal party by adding to the 55 members from Quebec a contingent of 116 other members, making a total of 171. The new Liberal family has still grown with the 1940 elections, when Quebec contributed 61 members out of 178 or 185, if the Progressive and Independent Liberals sitting on the government side of the house are included.
Therefore, the Liberal party has started to implement its armament programme after the elections of 1935, that is in 1937, while the new family had a decided influence on the old. That was the beginning of the Liberal government's evolution towards a policy of war.
As the moving power of the Liberal party's opportunism is now coming from a different direction, the Prime Minister immediately endorses the policy of the imperialistic group forming the majority and hardly conceals his relinquishment of former policy and his severance from former supporters. The Liberal party expounded its former policy to the French population in order to climb into power. To remain in power, it now endorses the policy of the other group. This purely opportunistic evolution is the direct cause of the violent conflict existing at present between our two main racial groups whose training is so profoundly at variance.
These are the ghastly straits into which the Liberal party's opportunism has enticed the Canadian nation by promises and pledges from which it now requests a release. Before imposing conscription on Quebec, we shall grant it a plebiscite. As the government will not be released from its promises and commitments regarding conscription by Quebec, but rather by the other provinces, this, in itself, evidences the opportunism and trickery of the Liberal party.
At this dangerous turning-point of our history, I believe, Mr. Speaker,' that all Canadians of good will, who are desirous of maintaining national unity, so indispensable in this hour of grave danger and who are desirous of not endangering our war effort unanimously supported for the fostering of the general interest, should react against this wave of opportunism which threatens to plunge us into disunion. We should all oppose the holding of this plebiscite which all groups of the Canadian population disapprove for various reasons.
The Address-Mr. Roy

The present trend of events more and more convinces me that conscription would be disastrous for our war effort as well as for the future of the country.
Popular confidence, especially among our youth, has been badly shaken by the pronounced depression of 1929 to 1940. Let us not forget that the financial interests, who have enlisted the conscriptionists as standard-bearers, have abandoned our youth to moral and physical suffering during that long period by the fact that they have deprived it of the enjoyment of our national resources which they make so much about to-day. What right have we, of forcing our youth to rush, on strange lands and at the cost of life, to the defence of those assets, a share of which was heretofore denied them?
The government has given us a foretaste of what may be expected if conscription is resorted to. On a request from Great Britain, they have sent bright and gifted young men to Hong Kong before they were properly trained. They were removed to China, lacking the necessary armament to bolster the defence of an insufficiently fortified outpost. May I be allowed at this point, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that about one hundred of these unfortunate young men came from the Gaspe constituency, to offer my sincerest sympathies to their families who endure such frightful anxiety and who dread the news they have been awaiting for nearly two months. We have to fear the recurrence of incidents of that kind if conscription for overseas service is enforced.
In view of the disunity now prevailing and increasing in alarming proportions from day to day, the best advice we could offer the government and the opposition, is to respect the pledges taken by both parties during the 1940 election. On this condition, it may yet be possible to maintain confidence, peace and harmony.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I wish to state that I shall vote against the main motion and the amendments because I am opposed to the plebiscite and to conscription, measures that I consider as inopportune.
I fail to see how else I could act. It would be useless to speak against conscription and then vote for the adoption of the speech from the throne announcing the holding of a plebiscite to grant the government the freedom they wish for imposing conscription when they please. We should fear, if this threat ever becomes a reality, to be accused of complicity and hypocrisy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I wish to express our deep gratitude to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the splendid harmony he has brought about among the nations with which we are now associated. For years he has sought to be friendly with the United States. He brought about trade agreements with that country; he established the British preference, and he maintained friendly relations with the British empire. He was the medium that brought the Americans and the British together, and I consider that the meeting of the leaders of those countries on the high seas was the work of our own Prime Minister. Hon. members will remember when the British empire was somewhat antagonistic toward Russia, and will also remember the attitude of this government, which sought to maintain friendship with Russia. To-day we are glad that this spirit guided our leader. I hate to think what might have happened if we had not dealt kindly with Russia in those times. Our relations with China have been almost perfect for many years, and now these countries are in harmony in support of the British empire.
The Prime Minister has been a master not only in international affairs but also in promoting unity within this country itself. He had at his side, of course, an equally strong advocate of unity in the person of the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. We in Canada ought to realize that in some respects the people of Quebec may be a little different from the rest of us. They left Europe three hundred years ago, and their songs and their hearts are all for Quebec. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) is of Irish descent. He puts on his orange lily and speaks at orange gatherings on the 12th of July. His heart goes back to old Ireland. I put on a bit of heather and march to The Road to the Isles played by the pipes; we sing the songs of old Scotland, an odd psalm and Mary oj Argyle. Our hearts go back to the land of our fathers. So it is with the Sons of England. Why, when you gather with the Sons of England in Toronto you would think there was no place on God's earth except England. But that is not so with the people of Quebec. They are more parochial; they are true to the country in which they live; they marry early, have large families, and think home is the ideal place. So we must accept them as they are. But this war is the war of Canada, and we are receiving splendid support from our Quebec friends. They are showing a spirit of true patriotism, and will continue to do so, but we must not expect them to love the British isles as you and I love them. Our

The Address-Mr. Blair
hearts and souls go back to Britain. If we thought anything might happen to Britain, we would be unable to express our feelings. Britain was the home of our fathers, and that makes a vast difference in our feelings toward it.
I do not like this defeatist talk that one hears almost everywhere one goes. Defeat is something we should never mention. It is true that other empires rose and fell. There was old Babylonia, but drunkenness and debauchery were the only things it wrote into history. It was weighed in the balance and found wanting. Then came the Persian empire. It wrote into history only one thing of importance, one thing that maintained it for many years, the word "truth". That word is still commonly used in the Liberal party. The people of the world had confidence in the Persians, but eventually they came to worship the god of Bacchus too freely and fell into drunken ways. Then came the Grecian empire. Their contribution was science and education, but they too fell by the wayside. They also worshipped the god of Bacchus too freely, and Alexander died a drunken wretch. Then came the Roman empire, and it established the word "law". Our laws are based almost entirely upon Roman law. We were part of the Roman empire for four hundred years. Four hundred years is a long time, equal to the time from the reformation to the present day. We fashioned our laws upon those of Caesar. We got our churches from the Romans, and the Roman empire lasted for many years because it had a more solid foundation than the previous empires.
We come now to our own empire. Why should it endure? It will endure because of the ingredients of which it is composed, because of the ideals and standards that go to make it up. We in the British empire have the word "truth" well established; that is well known the world over. We have the education and the sciences of the Greeks. We have a nobler, a larger vision; we have the love of humanity, and the brotherhood of mankind is stamped upon British people as it is upon no other race. We do not proclaim these things as much as we should among our own people. We do not altogether appreciate the opportunities we enjoy. For instance, there was Rufus Isaacs, who was a wharf rat. He went to India, where he stayed for a few months, returning to England as a waif, but eventually going back to India as viceroy. Opportunities of this kind are not accorded to the people of other nations. Take the Boer leaders; they were our bitter enemies; but after Britain defeated the Boers, they became true British subjects. We must remember that in the British empire there are practically no conquered races. They are given the privileges of freedom and citizenship and can rise to the highest levels. We saw Mr. Thomas sitting in one of the seats of this chamber not so many years ago. He was a blacksmith in England, and through his own efforts he rose to become minister of labour there, one of the highest honours his country had to give.
These are things that go to build up the heart and soul of an empire. But not only are we true to our own citizens; we have a kindly feeling toward all other nations. This is shown by those who rallied round us during this time of war. The other nations have confidence in the spirit of Great Britain; they have confidence in the truth of the British word, and they understand the kindly spirit that goes with it.
I believe we do not tell enough about our own race. Not long ago I asked a man where a certain German lived. That man said to me, "You know, he is a German, and we should take our hats off to Germans." I said, "I always touch my hat in deep respect to every race, but I take my hat off to none." He said to me, "They are above us in matters of culture, education and scientific development. What is your profession?" My reply was, "Well, I am a medical doctor." My friend said, "Where would the profession of medicine be without the Germans"-and he began to take his hat off. As a matter of fact he took his hat off two or three times, and asked me to follow suit. But I said, "Oh, no. Do you know about the plagues which have taken place in this world, and cut people down by millions? Do you know about smallpox, and do you know that the person who made a cure possible was Doctor Edward Jenner? Do you know that the circulation of blood was discovered by Harvey, an Englishman? Supposing I were called out to attend a case of appendicitis, and I had to go to a hospital, what would call the hospital for me but the invention of Alexander Graham Bell of Brantford, an old country Scot? Then, when I got to the hospital, who would disinfect all instruments used in the operation but Lord Lister of Edinburgh? When I put the patient on the operating table to be chloroformed, who gave us chloroform, if it was not old Doctor George Ferguson of Glasgow, the discoverer of anaesthetics? When I got my cheque for performing the operation, who would be behind that cheque? It would be William Paterson, a tramp from the highlands of Scotland, the founder of the Bank of England and all other banks."
The Address-Mr. Blair

We have a fine race of people, and we do not take our hats off to any. This ought to be made known. We do not tell our own people about our race, and I hate to see anyone sitting over here in sham modesty while we hear the Germans prate about their accomplishments, their culture and even their songs and music-and I do not like any of it very much. They say, of course, that it is better than ours, but so far as I am concerned it is not.
May I draw the attention of the house to the singing we hear from Toronto. Probably I should not criticize that city, but if one listens to his radio he will soon find that they do not even know how to sing God Save The King. They do not know the difference between "the king" and "our king". We must remember that when we sing "God save our king", the word "our" is the possessive, personal adjective, and refers to the personal king. When, as in the last line of our national anthem, we sing "God save the king", we are singing something altogether different. The expression "the king" is more comprehensive, including the British people, our institutions, our courts, our churches and everything else. But in spite of this fact we hear singing in churches and lodges-I was going to say in Toronto, a place where I often go-which does not seem to take notice of this fact; they sing the last line, "God save our king." While in Windsor I heard a judge of the supreme court singing the words "God save our king" in the last line of the national anthem, and I said to him, "Don't you think you are a little off the tune?"
I stand to attention when I hear the singing of "God save our king", but I stand doubly to attention when I hear the words "God save the king." And here is another thing: When we are singing God Save The King we mean that we are trying to cooperate with every form of democracy. Yet when our Prime Minister was elected by the largest majority ever accorded any prime minister, the men down in this front row got up and fold him to get out. They would not stand for his being Prime Minister; they wanted someone else in his place. I say that those men who wanted the Prime Minister to vacate his seat after the people elected him were all off the tune, and they did not understand the meaning of God Save The King.
There is a vast difference between "the king" and "our king", and we ought to recognize that difference. One should listen to those churches in Toronto. I did so, the last Sunday I was home. They were singing, "God save our king", and I said, "Oh. they are just those Irish Orangemen over in Parkdale." But

my wife was listening to the radio in the evening, and she heard the congregation at Old St. Andrew's singing the same way. So heaven help Toronto if they make no distinction between "our king" and "the king"! They sang it wrong in both churches.
When we sing God Save The King we should try to harmonize and put that thought into every speech made in the house. The House of Commons should be a great choir. When we rise in our places to make our speeches, are we singing God Save The King, or are we trying to disrupt? Are we trying to condemn the government unnecessarily, or are we trying to harmonize through the government a spirit of democracy and coop^ eration? Are we trying to sing God Save The King? I hear it sung in the churches, and I can think of no place it should be sung more frequently than right here in the House of Commons. This is the place where we should sing God Save The King. Every time a man rises in his place, I say, "Is he singing God Save The King when he is making his speech?" I appreciate the fact that frequently he is, but sometimes he is not.
I should not criticize Toronto, but its club rooms are dangerous places. I have great respect for the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson): I knew him years ago, and I consider him a noble leader. But he went to Toronto, and spent a night or two in those club rooms. After coming out he gave one of the silliest speeches possible, making references to friendship between the Prime Minister and the United States. It was a sort of political ballyhoo, and was done for political purposes. That speech was one of the hardest blows, not to him personally, but to the Conservative party.
The sooner we get together and realize that we have leaders, that we must stand behind them, that we must support them until the war is over, the better for all of us. After the war is over, do what you like with them; Vote them out when election day comes. That is the way to sing God Save The King.
The reeve in my home town is the hotel keeper. At the time of election I fight against him, but as soon as he is elected I shake hands with him and say "God save the king"- to myself, of course. I am a coroner and a health officer. I can send a man a summons to serve on a jury. If I am going to sing God Save The King I should enquire from him if service on the jury meets with his convenience. I should not be a dictator. Then I have the right to expect cooperation. We must have cooperation so far as possible, whether we are in office or whether we are members of an opposition. If we are going

The Address*-Mr. Henderson
to sing God Save The King we must have cooperation and harmony. I sincerely hope that this will be the key-note of every speech made in the house. If we are not in tune with that sentiment, we should be, and should be ready at all times to sing God Save The King.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, being a new member of this house I have not taken up much of its time in debate. I have done most of my talking to private members, the acquaintance of whom I have tried to make in committees and party caucuses. I have taken most of my problems to the departmental offices. I have taken this course because I sit on this side of the house where we are in such great numbers. I have thought it best to leave the talking to older members, more especially when I consider the great cost of carrying on these debates. I had thought that this debate would have been finished in three days, but it is now going into its third week. I am reminded of the advice given me by a good friend out west who quoted from a biography of Disraeli. When Disraeli was Prime Minister of Great Britain he was asked by a new member if he thought he should speak at the first session. Mr. Disraeli said: "Well, on the whole I think you had better not, for it is always better to have the people wonder why you do not speak in the house than to have them wonder why you do." I think that is pretty good advice for a new member.
I represent the constituency of Kindersley in Saskatchewan, named for Lord Kindersley, president of the Hudson's Bay company. I desire to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his government upon the contents of the speech from the throne. The mover and the seconder of the address in reply, the Prime Minister and the ministers of the government who have spoken in this debate, have made a splendid contribution in outlining our war effort to date and our future war plans. I came to this country some thirty-five or thirty-six years ago when thousands and thousands of immigrants were going into western Canada. We went 85 to 150 miles south of the railroad at Battle-ford and we considered ourselves real pioneers in those days. Among the farmers who settled there were many business men and we all worked together. As additional lines of railway were put through the country, we endeavoured to build for the future. Villages were put up, and banks, lumber yards, schools, churches, hospitals, flour mills and so on were built. Under the leadership of the Hon. Mr. Motherwell, the Hon. George Langley, the Hon. Mr. Dunning and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) we were helped by the provincial government to erect creameries and1 cooperative elevators. Manitoba under the leadership of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) and others carried on a somewhat similar programme.
We ploughed straight furrows; we tamed the wild lands; we built our homes and erected better schools, universities and so on. We tried to build a citizenship that would be an asset to all Canada. As time went on, more railroads were built through the district, and soon the 150 mile stretch I mentioned was crossed by eleven lines of railways. Mr. James J. Hill said that if these lands were properly tilled and cultivated, they would provide tonnage for a railroad not to exceed a distance of ten to eleven miles on either side.
In those days we had markets and we prospered. We got along quite well until 1911 when we had our first setback. Our lands depreciated at least $5 an acre under the defeat of reciprocity. The United States was the first to pass the act, but they left it on the books for a number of years and we enjoyed their markets and got on splendidly until 1917. At that time more markets were opened abroad and we were asked to produce more products. The west was opened up to a greater extent than it should have been. Some of the lighter land was broken that never should have been broken. In the district where I am farming we have heavy land, dark chocolate in colour, known as edge-grain soil. This soil ranges in depth from fifteen to ninety feet and is able to store considerable moisture. We shall be able to produce crops on this land for many years provided it is properly tilled and cultivated.
Conditions changed considerably during the dry years and during the economic war that preceded this physical war. We lost our markets during the depression and now we are faced with accumulated debts. Many of our farmers have had to go on relief while others have lived on their capital and profits made during better times. We had to ask for debt adjustments and readjustments. Banks and schools closed and many lost their homes. Federal, provincial and voluntary debt adjustments have run into several millions. We have been seeking monetary reform, lower rates of interest and assisted markets, but we still have in mind the establishment of a central bank. We feel that we should have this because, when the war is over, we hope to be able to bring debtor and creditor together. Only by doing that shall we be able to settle with most of our creditors at two dollars to one on occasions.
The Address-Mr. Henderson

With the help of these adjustments many of us were able to save our homes and we built up a morale that is becoming stronger day by day. The crops in 1939 were quite good and we managed to pay off some of our mortgage and machine debts. In the meantime, however, we have lost much money and many of our people. According to the last census the representation of Saskatchewan will be reduced by four, if the ratio with Quebec is applied. It would seem that our province is the dead-end province as it was called by one of the press representatives now sitting in the gallery. That may be the truth, but it hurts. We are, however, ready to stay on and win. This reduction in representation was referred to last night by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven), and I have his permission to associate myself with what he has said. I think Saskatchewan should receive the same treatment as has been given to Ontario on two or three different occasions. That province has been able to maintain its membership at eighty-two members and, according to my figuring, based on the Quebec membership the Ontario membership should be only seventy-four. If something could be done to equalize the representation as between the east and the west, it would help us very much.
I have heard it said on the floor of this house that if we cannot get on, we should get out. Even though our numbers are fewer, we are ready to remain loyal to Canada. Even though it happened that we were no longer in the federation, we would still be loyal ' to the empire and would continue to deal with the motherland via the Hudson Bay railway and to fight Hitler to the end to prevent his entry into our wheatlands. We have preached Canadian citizenship to all our people. In fact I have been doing this work myself more or less from coast to coast. After all, we are all good, loyal citizens.
Perhaps I may be permitted at this time to say a word with regard to the Hudson Bay railway. If Jim Hill had been permitted to exercise the charter he asked for in the early days, he would have built up an empire in that north country. He would have opened up those mineral lands just as he opened up the lands in the lake Superior district, and all this would have been greatly to our advantage. The mineral wealth of the pre-Cambrian shield has hardly been scratched, yet the two or three mines operating there have justified the expenditure twofold, and in any event it has been very largely paid for by western Canada lands. There is ample power in the north, and if through scientific development and discovery we should be able to have that transferred, it would help us industrially. We

have no great quarrel with labour and industry in this country. It is simply a question of agriculture having been the first to suffer and the last to recover.
I come now to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which has been referred to this afternoon, and which was passed under the administration of Mr. Bennett. Perhaps that is the act which my hon. friend opposite had in mind when he spoke of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, with its provisions extended under the present Minister of Agriculture, has done a lot of good, in the opening up of grazing pastures and the rehabilitation and reclaiming of many abandoned farm lands. Much more could be done along that line. Much more could be done for western Canada in the way of irrigation, if the waters were stored in Tramping Lake coulee and other large coulees. That would be better than paying money out for relief, and with irrigation we should be able to grow our feed, fodder and garden produce to make a livelihood on the prairies, without having to ask our eastern friends to come to our aid. The cheques that have been paid out by way of bonus have helped to raise the morale of our people and are much better than relief cheques. Rehabilitation would, I believe, be a splendid investment for the whole of Canada. We want to cooperate with all Canada, east and west, right across, in regard to agriculture, and so far as we are concerned we are quite prepared to assist the east with lower freight rates to aid in the movement of feed grain and fertilizer, and would support subsidies where necessary.
I believe that it would be a good thing to guarantee the price of live stock until one or two years after the war. I believe that would encourage our agriculturists to go into the raising of live stock more than they are doing to-day.
I should like to refer to the brief which was submitted recently to the wheat committee of the cabinet and the government by the 440 farmers from Saskatchewan, in which they asked for an initial payment of $1 a bushel for wheat, parity prices, and an amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act as outlined by my colleague the member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham). I had his permission to be associated with him in that, and I shall save time now by not going into the matter in detail. In my portion of the country, for which I can speak, we have every confidence in the wheat committee of the cabinet, which was headed last year by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), the other members being the Minister of Finance (Mr. FEBRUARY 17, 1942
659,
The Address-Mr. Ferron
Ilsley), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). We know they have our interests at heart just as they have at heart the interests of all Canada. They have a very difficult problem to handle, and we know, too, that they realize that our problem is great. We are not asking for anything unfair or that would make the west a burden on the treasury, but now after more than two years of war there is a great need for food for the armies, particularly in view of the one billion dollars worth of supplies that is being appropriated for Great Britain. During the first war the wheat board brought the price of our wheat down, but we believe the time has come when we should have fair play and a fair chance. We are quite prepared to cooperate with labour, with whom we have no quarrel at all.
Surely in the new order that is to come when the war is over, we shall be rid of tariffs and trade restrictions, as outlined by Prime Minister Churchill, President Roosevelt and our own Prime Minister, so that our goods will move freely into the world markets.
With regard to the plebiscite, I think that is the only honourable way of dealing with the situation. The plebiscite is not definitely conscription as yet, but I think the hands of the government should be freed so that if the need for conscription arises, the government will be free to bring it in. So far as conscription being an issue in the last campaign is concerned, in my constituency it certainly was an issue. My opponent came out for conscription in his first address, while another opponent of mine was said to be a pacifist. I supported one hundred per cent total war, with a balanced agriculture and industry, and man-power sufficient to provide all the required equipment and to keep our supply lines open.
All things considered, I think our war effort has been a splendid one for a small nation of eleven million people. I think it would be well if we were more tolerant with one another, and then we should get on better, particularly with an educational propaganda, in which, as I have good reason to know, most of our French-Canadian members have been engaged over the weekends, as I myself have been doing in the west. The first volunteer we had in my constituency in this war was a Ukrainian, a returned man. We have many Germans there too. A German lad came to my farm to take my first boy's place. He was born in Germany and naturalized in this country. He afterwards volunteered and is now overseas. We require a united people, and I think we can
accomplish that with proper educational propaganda. We should be tolerant of our peoples, as Churchill is tolerant of Eire, south Africa, India and all the peoples of the British commonwealth. I listened to his speech the other night when he spoke of divisions among us, and I think we should take that lesson to heart.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that we now have Japan arrayed against us, but we have the United States in the war on our side, with all her great resources, and I do not have any fear that we shall be able to equip China and Russia and the million and a half Poles who are anxious to be armed. I am sure also, without any question of doubt, that we shall be able to complete the job. I shall have pleasure in supporting the government on the main motion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the session of 1942 offers a very strange spectacle. That the opposition should blame the government because the speech from the throne does not provide for conscription for overseas service and that two or three conscriptionists in the Liberal ranks should join in this blame, is in no way abnormal. But that a dozen members professing anti-conscriptionist views, as I do myself, should rise against the government because the same speech from the throne leads them to expect recourse to conscription for overseas service, and that they should vote with the avowedly conscriptionist opposition, is something that cannot but disturb a mind as little complicated as mine.
I would not for anything in the world wish to offend a single one of these hon. gentlemen. I do not question their sincerity and I know they will pardon my telling them in all frankness that I fail to understand their conduct. I cannot understand their making a profession of confidence in the Prime Minister and ending it by saying, "I have my doubts." I cannot comprehend their making eloquent assertions that there is in this country only one party leader capable of giving to the nation a government that is wise and that truly conforms to the aspirations of those who really seek national unity, and then declaring that they will not support that leader. They describe as nefarious the policy advocated by the Conservative opposition and its leader, but when it comes to voting the address in reply to the speech from the throne they intend to place themselves at the side of the latter and to vote for and with him.
It is this confusion, Mr. Speaker, which prompts me to rise in my place and explain the vote I shall shortly be called upon to give. My views have not changed since the 1940

The Address-Mr. Ferron
election. I then solemnly pledged myself to oppose any measure providing for conscription of the youth of my country for service overseas, and to-day I say to the leader of the Conservative opposition (Mr. Hanson), "Go no further!" I say to him that he shall not pass with his amendment which contains the following clause:
Completely mobilize the wealth and material resources aDd, on a selective basis, the full man and woman power of the nation, to the end that the nation may wage total war in any theatre of war.
There is no doubt that this motion, particularly after the explanations subsequently given by the hon. gentleman who moved it, is one for complete conscription for overseas service. Moreover, it involves non-confidence in the only government in which I have confidence. For similar reasons I shall vote against the amendment moved by the leader of the C.C.F., the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) who likewise demands "total mobilization of wealth, industry and finance, as well as human resources."
Having voted on two occasions against motions requesting conscription for overseas service, my views in the matter can admit of no doubt.
I shall now revert to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. What does it contain? I see in it three main propositions: first, an enormous and total effort for our national defence, accompanied by a thousand sacrifices to protect our territory and help our allies resist the enemy across the seas; second, improved national selective service; third, the plebiscite.
Regarding the first proposition, I admit, Mr. Speaker, that the words "effort" and "sacrifice" are not very attractive. But thinking of the axis menace which is daily becoming graver, thinking of the enemy submarines prowling close to our shores, seeing our freedom in jeopardy and also pondering upon the value of this freedom which I heard my venerable parish priest, Canon D. Baril, appraise from the pulpit in the following words: "Never forget that under the shade of the British flag we enjoy a greater freedom than if we were free"; I would fear that if I gave a negative vote the people of my constituency and the people of my province, who want to neglect nothing to properly defend their homes, their farms, their churches, their parochial and municipal institutions and, above all, their freedom, would reproach me some day for not having agreed to those many sacrifices. In any event, I prefer being sorry for having done too much than feeling remorse at having done too little.

With respect to national selective service- for the defence of our country, be it understood-I strongly approve such a measure. I support it because it will allow farmers' sons who are indispensable to the operation of their farms-they are very numerous in my constituency-to remain on the land and produce the foodstuffs required to feed our armed forces, our factory workers and also our allies who are fighting the same fight as we are. I am in favour of selective service because I wish our hardy woodsmen to return to the forest at the proper season and get out the lumber so greatly needed for shipbuilding and countless other war purposes. In a word, I want every one to be kept where he is the most useful, in the best interests of this country.
I now come, Mr. Speaker, to one of the most controverted matters, the plebiscite. If I were to consider the feeling in my constituency as reflecting the opinion of Canada as a whole, I think I could say without any fear of being mistaken that a plebiscite is not necessary. On behalf of my constituents I would tell you: Our people want to win the war. They want to do their utmost to preserve our freedom. They are willing to accept the greatest sacrifices for the defence of our territory and they are voluntarily enlisting in great numbers to help our allies overseas. But among the numerous means of achieving victory, one only is distasteful to them: compulsion as regards overseas service. We have done our duty so far, and we are more than ever determined to do it in future. But my constituency is not the only one in the dominion, my province is not the only one in the confederation, and since the last general election many important events have happened. More than a dozen nations have been overrun by the enemy, the United States, then neutral, is now at war and Hong Kong and Singapore have fallen. In view of this situation, could I voice any objection to a question being put to the Canadian people? As regards the reply to be given, I intend to tell my constituents: "Consider the situation as it is to-day, and analyse all the facts until the date of the plebiscite. With your usual good judgment try to foresee the possible trend of the enemy action and then without passion and prejudice, vote according to the dictates of your conscience". That is the course I shall follow myself.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, and to summarize what I have said, let me state that I have always been, that I still am and that I shall always be in favour of sparing no effort for our national defence. I am opposed to conscription for overseas service, because it is

The Address-Mr. Corman
intrinsically recognized as harmful to Canadian unity and further because it has been proven quite unnecessary.
I shall vote against both amendments because they are in conflict with the latter principle, and also because they have the character of motions of want of confidence in a government to which the opposition itself cannot direct any sound criticism.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I shall vote for the address because I believe in preserving national unity; this I think I can do only by supporting my leader the Prime Minister as well as the man who has assumed leadership in my province, the honourable the Minsiter of Public Works and Transport (Mr. Cardin).
Before I resume my seat, I may say that if I had the needed authority, I would direct to my friends and colleagues from Quebec a last appeal as follows:	You as everyone
else have the duty of looking into the future. But on the other hand, you have no right to ignore the past of the two great leaders, I have just named. Both have reached their second quarter of a century of public life. And their past speaks for itself. With you I beseech Providence not to remove them from our midst, but when, to my great comfort, I see the principles of Laurier and Lapointe ever advocated and ever triumphant, I say: those are hot men who die forever. Their pleas for union, harmony and common sense remain alive in our memory.
I have just mentioned the name of the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe. Tribute has already .been paid to the memory of that great man; and in words that expressed my own thoughts much more fittingly than I could voice them myself. However it is my desire that the vote I shall give in a few hours, at the side of his son the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Lapointe) should be a tribute to his memory and to the principles of tolerance and harmony to which he devoted his life.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In rising to make my contribution in this debate my first words must be of congratulation to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I think the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier) did very well, as did also the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald). May I add that I have a very high regard for the hon. member for Brantford, since his riding lies
adjacent to the constituency of Wentworth which I have the honour to represent in this house.
Wentworth, as every hon. member knows, has been represented in this house for a long time, but this is the first occasion in some years when it has been represented from this side of the house. I do not, however, take the stand that I am here to speak exclusively for the Liberal party. I feel that I also represent the county of Wentworth as a whole.
May I at this point pay tribute to the late Gordon Wilson who represented this riding for twenty-four years. Although we disagreed politically, the late Gordon Wilson was a very fine man and highly regarded in his community.	.
Let me at the beginning inform the house of my views on the big issues now before us. I am personally in favour of total selective service for overseas or anywhere in the world. In that view I think I represent the great majority in my county, both inside and outside the Liberal ranks. Wentworth has a record of which any county might be proud. More than one hundred and twenty-five years ago people in the county of Wentworth were repelling a foreign foe. Her sons have taken part in every fight since, and the contribution she made to the first great war was no small or inconsiderable one. In Wentworth county we take the stand that the fight for Canada does not begin on the shores of Canada. Wentworth county boys have fought all over the world and are willing and anxious to do so at this time.
In making the statement that I am in favour of total selective service I am not influenced in any way by the committee of two hundred whose headquarters seem to be in Toronto and who apparently are backed by influential mining interests. As I see it, their patriotic zeal is not so much impelled by love of country as by love of power. I personally do not admire their super-patriotism; they are apparently willing to sit behind their golden towers on Bay street and try to force the boys to go and fight for them. It is all very well to wrap the union jack about their wealthy' well-fed persons and call on someone else's sons to defend their wealth. I think it very fine that we should have total selective service, but not because this specially privileged group wants it. Nor am I so sure that conscription is their real goal. I think conscription is really a red herring across the trail, which, if the signs were marked properly, would point to a return to the abuses of the last war. The committee of "two hundred" dress their front windows with conscription, but let us see what they have in the back of the shop. Concealed under the counters is
The Address-Mr. Corman

national government, and with that enormous power, and a little further back but ready to bring out later are such things as abolition of the excess profits tax and the destruction of the price ceiling. This committee of two hundred, who use conscription as a come-on, also have in mind the return of a great many things which made the last war linger in an unpleasant way in the nostrils of not a few people. We want no shameless exploitation of the war to make a new crop of millionaires, and we want no conscription under these terms. The purpose of this conscription ruse, as initiated from the "two hundred," is to get the gold crowd into power. If they get their way, the rest of us will be reduced as quickly as possible to economic vassalage. We shall become hewers of wood and drawers of water to Bay street.
I said I favour total selective service, and I do. But it should not be obtained by the means the Toronto group seek, namely, to ram it down our throats like a gestapo order. The proper way is to obtain it through a plebiscite. This government made certain definite pledges in 1940. I am not going to linger long over this point since it has all been gone over so often, but the government now asks to be relieved of its non-conscription pledges. When that release is obtained, as I believe it will be, then the government will be free to do as it sees fit.
When that release is obtained I intend to press for total selective service anywhere it is required at that time. Let there be no doubt how and where I stand on this. I want to see total selective service put into force by the will of the people of Canada; not instituted by a little group of fascist-minded people who would split the country wide open to get their way. It may be that in the matter of total selective service, properly and constitutionally introduced, I would go further than they, but I want to go about it in the democratic way, the Mackenzie King way.
Here I should like to read an article published in the Hamilton Spectator on January 23, 1942, in which the editor of that paper comments on the government's decision to take the plebiscite. The Hamilton Spectator is an independent newspaper; its views are read and respected by many people in Canada. The policy of the Spectator is directed by Mr. Fred Ker, an outstanding citizen of Hamilton, who has always been very proBritish and pro-empire, for which he is to be admired. His opinions are highly regarded. I quote the editorial:
Prime Minister King will seek an expression of the will of the people to determine their attitude on the issue of conscripting Canada's

man power for overseas service in this war. A plebiscite will be submitted to them in which they will be asked to release the government from any past commitments which restricted the methods of raising men in this dominion for military service.
In resolving to pursue this course, it is difficult to see where the Prime Minister is impairing this country's war effort or doing violence to empire unity. Rather does it appear that he is striving to prevent the very disunity and bitter division which some of his partisan opponents are charging him with fomenting.
Mr. ICing's course should appeal to all even-tempered persons as a reasonable one, and also the most satisfactory way of settling this issue. After all, there is no safer tribunal in a democracy than the people themselves. Their voice ought therefore to be heard; and the premier has ensured that it shall be heard. His present position is consistent with his past stand on this question. On the outbreak of war he told parliament that no conscription for overseas service would be enacted so long as his government was in power. Later he again said that he further construed the verdict of the people, in the general election of March, 1940, as a mandate from them that they were opposed to conscription for overseas service. In the face of those facts, he should not be expected to repudiate his pledges. Were he to do so, he might invite widespread discord and reap serious results. The Conservative party leadership and candidates made no issue of Mr. King's position at the last election. They stood indeed on the same anti-conscription ground.
The speech from the throne implies that an affirmative response is sought from the people; the government asks to be "released from any obligations arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service." Canada's war effort to date has not been either feeble or meagre; so far as it has gone, it has been wholehearted and generous. That Canada can enlarge this effort is admitted, and plans are now well advanced by the government to gear the country for total war. A policy of national selective service will soon be in operation whereby the federal authorities aim to place every available person in the job for which he or she is best fitted to serve. The human and material resources of the dominion will be totally mobilized to intensify the production of munitions and foodstuffs; the armed forces will be expanded, all with the purpose of giving the fullest aid to Britain of which this country is capable. Financial provisions are also to be made on an unprecedented scale, and the wealth of Canada is to be drawn upon by an orderly and equitable process to the utmost limit of its capacity.
Premier King's government need thus make no apology for the war-time leadership it has given the Canadian people. But it is not disposed to carry that leadership beyond the limits of the mandate the people have given it as regards conscription for overseas service-not until the people themselves authorize this step. If the plebiscite rejects compulsory selective service for overseas the fat will indeed be in the fire and it is hard to see how either a national election or a new parliamentary alignment that would disregard the plebiscite and enact conscription regardless of consequences,

The Address-Mr. Corman
could be avoided. Certain it is that one way or another we must have compulsory selection for service on any battlefront in the world.
Let me quote also part of another editorial from the Hamilton Spectator of February 10, which was written after the recent byelections :
The outcome, on the whole, is gratifying, inasmuch as it reflects an ability on the part of the people not to lose sight of the vital issues even in campaigns that were marked by such excesses of strife, party cleavage, class prejudice and confusion as these contests were. Representative government still means something in Canada, and the electors who voted yesterday have shown that they are quite capable of discharging their responsibility and not becoming lost in a foggy atmosphere of extreme partyism. In three constituencies, at least, they make it plain that their faith still reposes in the administration of Prime Minister King; and they have given him a mandate not only to carry on, but to prosecute Canada's war effort with increased vigour and adopt every measure that will contribute to that end.
The editorials I have just quoted represent the thought and feeling around Hamilton, and I have placed them on record in order that everyone in Canada may know the fair-mindedness of the press in the vicinity of Hamilton and their attitude toward the government's decision to take a plebiscite.
To turn to the question of money, it may become necessary that all profits be conscripted. We may reach the point where we shall so desperately need money to carry on this war that we must resort to this extreme expedient. We may have to take all capital, wherever we can find it, however we can get it, to prosecute this war to a successful conclusion. So we may have to have fiscal conscription, too. But this is nothing new or drastic; all these powers have already been given us under the National Resources Mobilization Act. We have only to take what is already ours. But we hear precious little from this total war group about this kind of conscription. Could it possibly be that, fearing the present government might just do that very thing, they want to get into power in time to stop that move? Conscript the boys by all means, they cry, but hands off our dividends!
I want to point out to those who seek conscription so eagerly and violently that conscription is only one part of a part of our war effort. The trouble is this. There are quite a few people in this country who think that the proper way to fight a war is to get a lot of men together in a hurry and send them some place; it does not matter where you send them, or why, or how; just send them, and the war problem is solved. To me, this ostrich-like attitude gets nobody anywhere.
First of all let us look at the man-power situation. We are already ahead of the last war, in the number of soldiers we have available for service anywhere in the world; in other words, we are better fitted in man-power in this war than in the last. But that is only part of it. In the last war our air service was very small in numbers. This time we already have raised over 100,000 men, and a steady stream of recruits is on the way. I do not have to emphasize the magnificent series of airports developed all over Canada since the beginning of the war. The erection of these is due entirely to the untiring work of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power). They deserve great credit, and I believe the people of Canada are realizing this more and more each day. It is a mighty effort in itself, and will do much to win this war, since it has been shown in past battles that an army without air force protection is helpless against the enemy. I sincerely believe that the air force will play a very large part in our future campaigns. Let us pay homage and respect to the gallant boys who fly against the enemy, especially the brave lads who fly the bombers over Germany. The people of Canada and of the world owe them their deepest gratitude.
In addition to the activities of the air force, let us not forget the activities of the Royal Canadian Navy. In our navy we have hundreds of ships manned by the gallant boys of Canada. Every day we read of their exploits and see where some Canadian destroyer or corvette has left its mark upon the enemy. According to figures recently released, we have over 30,000 men enlisted in Canada's navy, and it is expected that another 13,000 will be added this year, as soon as ships can be provided. The people of Canada, especially those who live inland, do not realize the enormous work our navy is doing. It is indeed a big war effort in itself; and if we only knew the hardships and privations that these men undergo, we would surely take off our hats to these gallant seamen.
Now let us come to agriculture. My constituency is mainly an agricultural one, and the contribution our farmers are making, not only in Wentworth but, I am sure, in every other constituency in Canada, is a vast one. To feed the defence forces of Canada is a huge war effort in itself, let alone sending enormous quantities of wheat, pork, eggs, cheese and canned fruits and vegetables to Britain to feed our brothers in arms overseas. The farmers are certainly doing their part. May I interject at this point that I believe the government should have some yardstick
The Address-Mr. Corman

for the postponement of the training of farmers' sons who are really producing agricultural products for the winning of the war. For instance, I would suggest that the last boy on the farm should not be taken; and in the case of a large farm, where two boys are producing twice as much, I think there should be a further postponement. I feel sure that if a yardstick for postponement were established, there would be less confusion in the minds of our farmer friends as to the calling of their sons for military training. As it is now, they cannot get help on the farms and are worried continually that their sons will be called, leaving them with no help. I agree with the policy of the government that men in industry, really doing a war job in the manufacture of munitions, should receive postponement of training, and I believe this is being done at the present time. I would suggest also that the age limit in the proclamation be raised to thirty-five, because I know there are many single men in Canada above the age of twenty-four who are doing very little to support our war effort. I believe these men should be called before farmers' sons are interfered with, and I would ask the government to take this into serious consideration.
Part of my riding is one of the most highly industrialized portions of Canada. At a later date, and in a later speech, I hope to make more extended reference to Wentworth county, of which I am proud. But I may say now that the workers in Wentworth who are turning out the sinews of war very much resent the allegations of the total war committee, who see no other effort in this war but military enlistment. The workers believe that the man behind the man behind the gun is important also. I do not < intend1 to dwell on the war worker unduly, but I do say that Canada's whole war production has been magnificent. Starting from nothing we have reached a productive capacity little short of amazing. There has been no industrial development like it in the history of this or perhaps any other country. This is due to the management of the present government, and especially to the work of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. If you seek to blame any administration for its shortcomings, as the opposition is only too ready to do, then you must also give credit to the administration under which such vast strides have been made.
Then there is the question of finance. To me this is a highly important part of our effort, and great credit must be given the government for their assistance to Great Britain at this time, in the gift of a billion

dollars and the lending of $700,000,000 without interest. I have not time to go into the question of the financing of this war, but it is reaching unbelievable proportions. The ' time may come when the money system should be changed. For instance, why not have an internal currency separate and apart from our external currency for the payment of imports and exports? In other words, why not arrange with the ether allied nations to agree on an allied dollar, to be used for international purposes only? If we had such a system, we could do pretty well what we liked1 with our internal dollar, controlled, of course, by loans and taxation. With the government's present policy of a price ceiling, we could have controlled inflation.
While dealing with the subject of finance,
I should like to protest in the strongest possible terms against the decision of the wartime prices and trade board to subsidize the importation of canned grapefruit juice. In the first place, this commodity should be placed on schedule 1 under the Foreign Exchange Conservation Act, and therefore would be embargoed. However, as it is allowable for imports, I can see no reason why the people of Canada as a whole should pay somewhere around $200,000 a year subsidy to United States importers.

In conclusion, I want to repeat that I am for total selective service of man-power, and woman-power if necessary, to win this war. I agree to some extent with the subamendment in believing that if we are to have conscription of man-power we should also have conscription of wealth and industry. I believe that everyone should put everything he has into a common effort to win this war. I also believe that any young man's life is worth more than all the money in the country, and that we should have equal sacrifice as nearly as possible for everyone. I have sufficient faith in our leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), to carry us through to victory, and I would ask the people of Canada at this time to place their faith in him, because I am convinced he is the only man in Canada who can keep Canada united successfully to prosecute this war.

The Address-Mr. Tremblay
Five times my leader has been returned to parliament by the will of the people. I have, therefore, more faith in the man who has had five mandates from the people than anyone else in Canada I know of. I intend to vote for the plebiscite, and ask the people of this country to vote "yes," so that the government's hands will be free to do what they think is best for our nation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1940 it has seldom been my privilege to take my seat in the house. I must admit that while I may be almost a veteran in the house, I almost feel that I am making another maiden speech, and that indeed I am desperately young.
May I apologize to hon. members for not having had the time in preparing my few remarks that I should have liked to have. I take great comfort however in seeing you, Mr. Speaker, in the chair. For the first time in my experience in the house I am going to attempt to deliver my speech in English, without the aid of notes.
Since June, 1940, I do not believe I have been in the house more than half a dozen times, and many changes have occurred since that date. May I take a moment, however, to add an expression of deep regret upon my failure to see in his seat, where particularly we Quebeckers were so happy and proud to see him, the late Minister of Justice, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. In these times of struggle, these tragic times, he made a great contribution to Canada's effort. In Quebec he was not only considered our leader, but recognized as a great Canadian. When we fail to see him in his seat we are indeed reminded of our great loss.
I had not intended at first to speak in this debate. From the camp in which I am now on duty I followed as best I could the trend of discussions in the house. I have been gratified and happy to see so many of my French-speaking fellow citizens from Quebec voicing their views and, under circumstances such as we have to-day, they did well to do so.
It is not my intention to add anything new to the debate, because I believe practically all shades of feeling in Quebec have been expressed, and other hon. members from other parts of Canada have spoken for their constituencies. I wish, however, to be somewhat outspoken concerning my stand on several points which I shall now detail.
First, I wish to consider Canada's war effort. Then I shall discuss Quebec's participation, and make some observations about Quebec, a province which in my estimation is not understood in every quarter of our country. I
desire to point out that not only am I opposed to compulsory military service for overseas, but in such opposition I am expressing the views of my fellow citizens in Quebec. I wish to say why that is so.
Let me add that we shall carry on. We are doing our very best, our utmost, for the great cause of civilization, the cause of freedom of mankind which our leaders in Quebec and other leaders across Canada have asked us to support, to fight for. I shall also say why we take this stand.
For the past several months I have been stationed outside my own province, and for the last four months I have been living in close proximity to the queen, and so greatly discussed, city of Toronto. I am perfectly happy to be there, and I am doing my utmost to understand a mentality different from that found in Quebec. As a matter of fact I sometimes have the impression that one is as far from the other as the north pole is from the south. If narrow-minded citizens are to be found in the province of Quebec, they are just as likely to be found in the queen city, in any other province of the dominion or in any place in the world.
On January 26 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) attempted to answer the question that everyone in Canada seemed to be asking-what is Canada doing; what is our navy; what is our army; what is our air force? This question was being asked during the election campaign, and I find the answer given by the Prime Minister reported on page 36 of Hansard. He said in connection with our navy:
At the outbreak of war, there were some 20 ships and less than 2,000 men in the Royal Canadian Navy.
At the beginning of 1940 the navy had grown to 80 ships, and over 5,000 men; at the beginning of 1941 the numbers had risen to 175 ships, and 14,800 men. At the beginning of this year the navy comprised over 350 ships and 27,600 men.
With reference to the army he said:
At the outbreak of war the permanent active militia, as Canada's regular army was then called, included about 4,500 men. By the end of 1939, the Canadian Active Service Force, to give the armv its name at that date, had increased to 64,000 men. The first Canadian division had just arrived in Britain.
At the close of 1940, the active army included almost 170,000 men. A Canadian corps of two divisions had already been formed in Britain. Canadian troops were also on active service in Newfoundland, the British West Indies and Iceland.
At the close of 1941, there were more than 260,000 men in the Canadian active army, enlisted for service in any part of the world. About half this number were on active service outside Canada. A third infantry division, an
The Address-Mr. Tremblay

armoured division, an army tank brigade, forestry troops, and other specialized units, and thousands of reinforcements were in Britain, in addition to the original corps of two divisions.
About the air force he said:
At the outbreak of war the active strength of the Royal Canadian Air Force was some 4,000, all ranks. By the close of 1939, the strength had risen to over 8,000; by the close of 1940, it had reached 43,000; by the close of 1941, it exceeded 100,000 men.
Is that the total of Canada's war effort? I could read pages and pages of facts cited by the right hon. the Prime Minister, which demonstrate that Canada's war effort is large and magnificent. Its magnitude has been recognized and praised by people outside Canada as well as throughout the world. The Prime Minister referred to another aspect of our war effort, as reported on pages 35 and 37 of Hansard. He stressed the importance of our contribution in food, munitions, machines, ships, aircraft, tanks and other supplies of all kinds. Canada's war effort in these items is surprising and amazing. As I said, we have had testimonials from outside Canada, and we find one in the Toronto Telegram, that paper so often spoken of. Commenting upon a visit of what they termed key men to Toronto arsenals and munitions plants, the Telegram had this to say on January 26:
Key men of democracy's arsenal pay Toronto surprise visit.
Munitions experts from U.S. tour Toronto war plants are impressed with work.
"Most encouraging," Roosevelt's personal representative says-praise for women.
Here is what Milo Perkins, personal representative of President Roosevelt had to say:
"Our inspection of your plants was very interesting," he said. "We covered a lot of territory in the brief time at our disposal. I *was particularly pleased with the plant of Research Enterprises Limited. It is a manufacturer's paradise. It is just w-hat a plant should look like. The trouble with many of our plants is that they are old and have not always the modern machinery we saw to-day.
I was also greatly impressed by the number of young women working in the plants we visited. They all seemed capable and intelligent. They appear to be fine types of citizens who are doing important jobs and doing them well."
These experts stated that they had learned a lot in their few hours' visit to some of our war plants. The article continues:
The size and production capacity of the plants inspected yesterday was both surprising and encouraging, Mr. Currie, the president's representative, said.
"We have learned a lot which we can't discuss at this time," he added. "I will say, however, that it is most encouraging to the people of the United States to realize how much Canada is capable of doing towards our common cause, in the Pacific and in the Atlantic."

Testimonials of that kind are much more comforting than some of the speeches which were made in some of the constituencies in the last by-elections. They are more comforting than some of the things we heard from a gentleman who has been in public life but who, I hope, is not likely to be in public life very soon again. He belittled Canada's effort, so much so that true, loyal Canadians had reason to be ashamed and veil their faces. Fortunately that gentleman encountered defeat. Then why ask for conscription? Why give the world the impression, or at least try to give the impression, because as a matter of fact you cannot fool the world, that Canada is not doing its utmost? Why deny the facts? Why insist on having conscription? A headline on the other side of the very same page of the very same newspaper might help us to understand why. The article is entitled, "Defence, excess profits and corporation taxes said in line for boost-Canada's war financing problem also likely to bring further controls on buying." Why should the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) tax excess profits heavily? Why should the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) put a limit on contractors' profits? Was the Canadian government not doing that already? It is a hundred chances to one that but for that gentleman to whom I have referred we would never have heard about conscription at a time when things were evidently going very nicely and when Canada should have been more than proud of the gigantic effort we were making. Why bring up this conscription question which, it has been said in this house by some of my fellow members from the province of Quebec, could only bring about misunderstanding and hurt Canada's war effort as a whole?
In the province of Quebec we have many a reason and every reason to be not only happy but very proud indeed of the efforts of our French-speaking province in this war. May I quote what the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) said the other day, as reported at page 250 of Hansard of February 2. He was speaking of Canada's efforts during the last war compared with this war and said:
I am reminded of figures which we sometimes forget, that of all those gallant gentlemen who went in the name of Canada in the last war, I believe only about 125,000 were Canadian-born.
In the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, we can say that we are all Canadian-born. In the other English-speaking provinces of the dominion, in the city of Toronto, for instance, a large proportion of the citizens came to Canada quite recently, within the last ten or fifteen or twenty or thirty years. They were born overseas. Some have been born in Canada of parents who came from overseas.

The Address-Mr. Tremblay
I perfectly understand the feelings of these citizens of Canada and can well understand their anxiety in matters where Great Britain or the British empire is deeply concerned. I have sometimes been shocked at hearing what I had considered good Canadians talk of this Canada of ours as "this country". Evidently their affections, their heart and soul, were first of all with the old land, England. Their parents, their brothers and sisters and other members of their families may be over there.
But with the citizens of Quebec province it is different. In Quebec, especially in the rural constituencies such as Dorchester county, which I have the honour to represent, practically every citizen's father is lying in the parish cemetery. His grandfather might lie there, and his great grandfather. We are rooted in the Canadian soil and have been for two or three centuries. We have no other country. We have no motherland except Canada. Canada is our only motherland. It has been said that we in the province of Quebec are not world-minded. We cannot be. Nor are we empire-minded. We are Canada-minded, and it must be said too that we are a bit Quebec-minded. Sometimes I have had the question put to me: What is the matter with Quebec? Well, here is one answer, and I hope when I have given it, that whenever the question is asked again throughout this Canada of ours, what is the matter with Quebec? We might answer with another question: What is the matter with you? Quebec, a province composed of wholly Canadian-born, has given to the navy up to October 31, 1941, 4,077 recruits; to the army, almost 50,000 recruits; to the air force, almost 800 officers and to other ranks of the air force over
11,000	voluntary recruits. I have been asked not to give exact figures, but we can put the total number of enlistments in all arms of the service as pretty close to 70,000.
We have had some handicaps; we surely have. May I quote from an article entitled "Language Difficulty" in Maclean's magazine of August 1, 1941, and let me say that I personally had experience of cases over a year and a half ago of many French-speaking electors-welders, electricians, radio operators and so forth-who wanted to join the Royal Canadian Air Force but were refused because they could not understand English. These are facts of which I know. This is what Maclean's magazine says:
Take, first, the air force. In setting forth qualifications for young men desirous of becoming pilots, observers, gunners and navigators, an educational standard was necessary. So one was written into the rules. It entailed, among other items, fluency in English, in which language the commonwealth countries happen
to be conducting the war. Other yardsticks were required and these, too, were established. In general they may be described as those of the Ontario educational system. They were not set up by the politicians, but by the qualified top men of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
These are facts.
But the major language of Ontario is not the language of Quebec, and the education standards of Ontario are not those of Quebec either. Quebec schools of the higher learning have leaned from the time of their inception toward what are generally called the liberal arts. Not until June, 1941, for example, did Laval university produce a course leading to the degree of mining engineer satisfactory to the Corporation of Professional Engineers of Quebec. Ontario, on the other hand, carries the student along more rapidly in the subjects classed under the science heading.
That is one handicap. Nethertheless we can boast of this, and I may give the testimony of the provincial secretary of Quebec, speaking on November 24, 1941, of what is being done in that province:
Ships are now being built in Canada in such numbers and at such speed that soon our yards will be turning out a volume of tonnage comparable with that produced in England. Much of that shipbuilding is now being done in the province of Quebec.
You all know of the expansion of the Canadian navy: from thirteen vessels to about four hundred, in two years, is not a bad record. Not only have many of those vessels been built, but much of their equipment, including guns of various calibres, has been made right here in the province of Quebec. Ships have been manned with competent officers and crews found and trained on the banks of the St. Lawrence river.
Rifled cannon barrels, as well as the controlling mechanism, consisting of wheels and cogs, springs and pinions and levers, are being fashioned by Quebec craftsmen who are conscious of their responsibility. They know that the failure of a part may mean the failure of a gun, and the failure of a gun may mean the failure of artillery support for their own brothers and sons locked in battle with the enemy.
High-speed tanks, too, are rolling off the assembly lines right here in Montreal. ... In Quebec we are producing more in a week than was produced in a month in the last war.
So much for what we are doing in a material way. Now, what about manpower? Quebec can justly boast that it provided the first full regiment of infantry in Canada. It was a French-Canadian regiment.
Le Regiment de Maisonneuve.
It was recruited to full strength under its gallant leader, Colonel Robert Bourassa, himself a veteran of the last war, and who unfortunately, after proceeding to England with his unit, has now been invalided back and lies here paralysed. He led the van of Canada in recruiting and the sympathy of all Canadians must go out to him now, to console him in his suffering.
His was the first regiment. The two regiments which followed in recruiting to full
The Address-Mr. Tremblay

strength were one from Ontario and the other one again from the province of Quebec. Several other regiments, both English-Canadian and French-Canadian, have gone from this province.
These are facts which are known to all and which it is right to recall in times like these.
That is what Quebec has done. Now, what is Quebec doing? We are increasing our production. We can boast of one plant in particular, which is being operated in Sorel, the city of the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), which experts marvel at, and the war products of which are going all over the world. The premier of the province and all our leaders, religious, civil and political, have brought home to Quebec the ideals for which we and our allies are fighting. Recently the premier of Quebec said:
More than ever determined that the war must bring us triumph, Canada's largest province is leaving no stone unturned in seeking means to have its share of the national effort in keeping with its important place in confederation. Its sons, worthy representatives of whom the old French province may well be proud, are serving under the colours on divers fronts. Behind them stands, solidly to a man, the whole population of their province, with an indomitable will that their effort under arms be rendered effective by the total employment of every resource of the home front-mines, forests, the land, production and service -to the great end of victory.
Progress is enormous in every department of our governmental service and every domain of our economic life. Our proverbially sound business and industrial organization has been raised to unprecedented proportions, and in its entirety is being utilized in the battle for freedom.
Our beloved leader whose departure we regret so much, and whom I mentioned a while ago, led us towards this war effort, and we are proud of it. He fought prejudices wherever he met them, and we belong to his school. We are proud to be his disciples.
But there are things we cannot understand; things in which we cannot acquiesce. I have reference to the sort of appeal to prejudice w'hich has been made in recent by-elections against the province of Quebec, belittling everything and ignoring totally the contribution of that province in the present war. One cannot believe for a minute that speeches such as that reported in the Toronto Evening Telegram., made by that dear Doctor Shields, at Aurora, can improve the situation in circumstances such as we are living under to-day. I would not care to put any of his divagations on Hansard.
