speechtext:
But if such men really wanted to contribute to Canada's effort, they would not preach disunity; they would avoid everything tending in that direction.

Now, sir, why is the anti-conscription sentiment so strong in the province of Quebec? That is a known fact; it has been so apparent in the house since this debate started, that Quebec stands to a man against conscription. We are against conscription. Why? Precisely by reason of the means and ways by which conscription was just thrown at us in 1917. We are willing to do, we are indeed doing all that is humanly possible. But hon. members may remember the discussions that took place in this house in 1917 and before the general election of that year on conscription. Quebec then was the billy-goat. The way conscription was put into force in Quebec was atrocious, just terrible. There was an evident will to misunderstanding. In our little parishes you can go into practically every house in the county of Dorchester and in every rural county in Quebec and they will tell you what seem like wild stories; they will tell you of their youngsters, seventeen and eighteen years old, quite a number of whom had hardly left their own parishes before, had never seen a soldier or a khaki uniform. They were working on the farms with their fathers -and that is another respect in which Quebec may differ from other provinces; the son to-day is working his father's land, and his father may be the second or third generation on that same land. Well, what happened when conscription was brought about? Military police were sent throughout those Frenchspeaking parishes in Quebec province and at night pulled these boys right out of their beds and, without being able to give any explanation of what was happening, brought them down to the drill hall. It is this procedure which brought about this testimony which I found in Maclean's magazine of January 15, 1942:
No matter how things may appear on the surface in Quebec, the fact remains that the word "conscription" is still the issue of the hour, even with our own Pacific coast an imminent danger zone. And yet, strange to say, it is not the question of service to the state or the democratic cause which is the burning issue, but the use of a word which has come to enjoy a grisly connotation in French-Canadian minds . . .
Many people believed the Jap attack on the United States would bring about an immediate volte face. It did not, with the new battlefield of the Pacific barely opened the Hon. Arthur Matthewson, English Protestant provincial treasurer, and a Black Watch officer of fine fighting record from the last wrar, was on the air speaking of "sinister forces" at work to destroy national unity through their insistent drive on this one bogey-word. He Bpolce of certain sections of the press. It is a well-known fact that Matthewson was gunning primarily for the Montreal Gazette and, in lesser degree perhaps, for Jean Charles Harvey's Le Jour, the very name of which is anathema to French-

The Address-Mr. Weir
speaking leaders of church and public life. The Toronto Telegram may also have been included.
All that is associated in our mind in Quebec with the personality of Arthur Meighen. Can you imagine anything worse? He was, rightly or wrongly-we are convinced rightly-blamed for what happened in 1917. At any rate it would have been sinister to see that same Meighen returned to this house. - This writer appreciates that so well that he said:
The latest point is Arthur Meighen. Feeling here is that if the Conservative party had definitely wanted to assure itself of no seats in Quebec at the next federal election, even though Meighen steps down before that time, it could not have made a better leadership selection.
That is a truism in Quebec. How could well-intentioned people expect, or how could it be explained, that those who undertook that conscription campaign, knowing these facts, really wanted to increase Canada's war effort? They merely wanted to secure power; that is quite obvious. Fortunately for Canada, fortunately for peace and good understanding throughout the country, the good and sensible citizens of Quebec were guided rather by common sense than by appeals to prejudice. Let us hope this may indeed constitute a lesson, painful as it may be, which will assure harmony and goodwill and cooperation from all sections of Canada.
It has been said, I have heard it in the house since this morning, that another good, kind-hearted Conservative member would resign his seat in the house to give Mr. Meighen another chance. I say-Give Canada a chance, not Mr. Meighen. Here I might make a practical suggestion. I am sure he would be defeated anyway in any constituency in Canada wherever he decided to run; why sacrifice one of the remaining Conservative seats in the house? We have a county open in Quebec, Charlevoix-Saguenay; send him there; the result will be the same.
The reason why we in Quebec like the present Prime Minister and support him and have confidence in him is just because of the psychological fact that he understands Quebec, or at least seeks to do so; he is fair; he is just; that is his record, and we are prepared to support him again, even if we have one or two defections.
I should like to quote from the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 12, following the recent by-elections.
In countries where the British flag waves no politician ever permanently wrecked his career by taking a courageous stand in a good cause which failed at the moment to prevail. Let Mr. Hepburn and Colonel Drew remember the career of Lloyd George. In 1900 he narrowly escaped death at the hands of an irate mob
in Birmingham, who resented his pro-Boer sympathies, and within eight years he was chancellor of the exchequer and the idol of the working classes of Britain.
They need not have cited this example; they could have mentioned the case of the present Prime Minister, in 1917, which would have given the same lesson to Mr. Drew and the others.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the fact that lion, members have unanimously permitted me to speak beyond my allotted time. I appreciate it the more because it is unlikely that I shall be back here very often; that may account for the generosity of my hon. friends.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of hesitancy that I rise to continue this debate this evening, a debate which has been going on now for some time. I am sure every phase of the discussion has been pretty well covered, and no doubt most hon. members would like to bring the debate to a close as quickly as possible. I should like to take this opportunity to extend my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. That they acquitted themselves well, no one will deny.
On this, as on other occasions, the speech from the throne provides an opportunity for the widest possible range of discusssion. Anything may be talked about during this debate. It is only natural, however, that the discussion so far should have been devoted largely to the one matter that has created the greatest interest, not only in this house but throughout the country; that is, the reference to the holding of a plebiscite asking the people of Canada to release the government from previous pledges made in connection with one phase of Canada's war effort. It is only natural that the discussion should largely centre round that point, and I should like to confine my remarks this evening more particularly to the same matter.
The constituency which I have the honour to represent in this house is for the most part Anglo-Saxon, and is looked upon as such. At the same time it contains numbers of French, Belgians, Icelanders, Ukrainians, Hut-terites, Germans, and some Czechoslovakians and Norwegians-all Canadians, I may say, but I merely mention them to indicate the complexion of the constituency. While it is trpe that the Anglo-Saxon group is in the majority, nevertheless the other groups make up well-nigh forty per cent of the population of my riding, and of this number the French-Canadians form the largest group. Here again these French-Canadians are representative not only of the province of Quebec but also of France itself.
The Address-Mr. Weir

Naturally there is in my constituency as wide a division of opinion on the issue of conscription for overseas service as is manifest throughout the country at this time. Even so, I have had Frenchmen come to me and say they were in favour of conscription. On the other hand I have 'had English people come to me and say they were opposed to conscription. I had an opportunity to talk with one man who has lost a son in this war. I discussed with him what the government was doing, what its war programme was, and what the programme was for the future. I tried to place it before him in as reasonable a manner as possible. He was a man with a good many contacts among the people, and when I got through I asked what he thought would be the attitude of the people with whom he was in contact with respect to the government's conduct of the war. His reply was that if the people were told what I had told him on that occasion, he thought the vast majority would agree with what I had said.
This conversation brought home to me one other point; that is, the value of the instrument of propaganda in this war. I fear that we have failed to tell the people of this country about Canada's war effort in such a manner as to drive it home and cause them fully to realize what this war means not only to Canada as a nation but to each person individually. Probably we as members of parliament have failed to do our part in this regard, more particularly among our nonEnglish-speaking Canadians. In time of war the instrument of propaganda is so important that I am bound to say I think we should make the best possible use of it.
There is another point I should like to mention, which I fear is not fully appreciated, and again this arises in connection with the French-Canadians in my own constituency. A number of them were called back to France at the time of the last war, to fight with the French armies. Later they returned to Canada. These men are as true Canadians as one could find anywhere, but to-day they are mystified and bewildered as to just what is going on and just what is going to happen. To some extent it is their desire to help the free French, but it is difficult for them to realize exactly what has taken place.
I mention these few points merely to aid in appraising the situation that exists in Canada to-day, because I am sure what I have said with respect to my own constituency could be repeated with respect to other constituencies throughout Canada, in greater or less degree. I keep asking myself, then, what there is to be gained by forcing the issue of conscription at this time. If it would help

win the war, or if it would shorten the length of the conflict, there might be some purpose in urging its adoption now. It is doubtful, however, whether it would do either at the present time. It is admitted that we could not satisfactorily conscript men for the air force or the navy; in fact it is not necessary to do so, since men for these services are coming forward voluntarily in greater numbers than can be accommodated and trained. Then, under our National Resources Mobilization Act the government already has authority to call men and women for home defence, and to place them in any kind of service the state may require. If this authority is not being used to the extent it should be, there may be ground for criticism. That authority could easily be extended to take in a much wider age group, if necessary, and it could be expanded in other directions. If necessary, we could call up men and train them for four or six months, giving them a thorough training and then letting them return to civilian life. This could be done with group after group, making certain that we would have a large number of men in this country thoroughly trained at least for home defence.
The issue, therefore, comes down to the one question of selecting men by conscription for overseas service only. In other words, its application would affect only that group of men whom we might desire to send beyond our territorial waters. The enactment of conscription is not going to change the situation with respect to the postponement of military service, or the method of dealing with conscientious objectors. These items are details of what we already have, and would not likely be changed by the extension of conscription for overseas service. We would likely continue to call up men by age groups; so that feature of the present policy would not be changed.
Here we are; we have, on the one hand, those who propose conscription for overseas service, regardless of anything else; and we have on the other another group just as strongly opposed to conscription as those who are in support of it. The two groups are as far apart as the poles.
Then, also, the people of this country had commitments made to them during the last election by at least the government and the official opposition, to the effect that no conscription measure would be enacted. I should think, sir, that those who supported the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or Doctor Manion during the last election campaign, would all welcome the opportunity of being relieved of the commitments made at that time. Anyone who claims that conscrip-

The Address-Mr. Weir
tion was not an issue in the last election is not telling the truth. For my part I tried to keep it from being an issue; but when a former cabinet minister came to my constituency, visited certain districts, and raised the issue in those places, I had to refer to it as well. I did so simply by reading statements made in this house by the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. I said that I did not know what the future had in store for us, or what changed conditions might bring about, but there was a statement made by a responsible minister of the crown, and as such it must be accepted, for the time being at least, as a matter of government policy.
I was not aware of the position taken in this regard by my opponents in the last election. For the most part I had thought that they, too, had refrained from making it an issue in that campaign. I found, however, in the local press, the week preceding election day, that both of my opponents, in a paid advertisement over their own names, and over the signatures of their respective associations, declared themselves in those advertisements as being opposed to conscription.

The Conservative party and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. We thus have these two points of view which, as I have mentioned, are as far apart as it is possible to be. We have the commitments which were previously made, and now we have these impassioned and emotional appeals from both sides, appeals which are only opening the gulf wider.
In the face of this turmoil and excitement, and having regard to the experiences of the past, can anyone contend that an appeal by way of plebiscite back to the people is not the sane and reasonable course to pursue? The gulf is too widely open to risk taking any other choice. For my own part I am supporting the proposal for a plebiscite, and I shall ask my constituents to relieve the government of the pledges previously made. I would appeal to them, regardless of their political faith, or to what race they may belong, to support this plebiscite and to vote wholeheartedly to give the government full authority to proceed with the prosecution of the war in whatever manner may be necessary, as occasion arises.
I do not think we can fail to keep in mind what happened in Australia during the last war. In that country, on two different occasions a vote of the people was taken with respect to conscription, and the sending of men outside of that country. On both those
occasions it was defeated. The second time the proposal was made the government gave the measure its wholehearted support, and yet it was defeated by a larger majority than it had been on the first vote.
Having said that, I should like to say something along a little different line. I believe there is some criticism which can be made, and I am surprised that in this debate some reference has not been made to some of these matters. The National Resources Mobilization Act gave authority to call men and women in Canada for any purpose the state might require. I am bound to say that I do not think this authority, so far as the direction of man-power is concerned, has been exercised to the extent it could have been, or to the extent the country expected it would be.
I recognize immediately that it is not easy, and that it takes time to redirect people to classes of work other than those to which they have been normally accustomed. In the province from which I come there is a shortage of men on the farms. That, I believe, is recognized more and more throughout farming areas all across Canada. There is also a reported shortage of men for bush work, and also a shortage of men for some other lines of work. At the same time there are a number of men probably unfit for military service, and unfit to undertake heavy manual labour, who are without jobs. Perhaps we can look upon them as the nonmanual-labour type of men. These men, however, are useful, and they could do much, if they were directed to where there is work to be done. I have had letters from and conversations with travellers who have been laid off. I have talked to men who were semi-retired office men, who are looking for something to do. Apparently as yet we have no plans to use them. I am bound to say this is a feature of our man-power situation which deserves more attention.
Then there is the question of conscientious objectors who were required to perform some service for the state. In Manitoba, for the most part they have been used in the national parks. There is no doubt that they did good work and that they were easy to handle. That kind of work, however, can wait. These men must be put to more useful employment. Under the circumstances which existed last year I am free to confess I do not know to what other type of work they could have been turned. But I feel they should be put to something more useful in the future.
I realize here again-and I do not wish to be misunderstood in this regard-that there are difficulties in the way of utilizing these people.
The Address-Mr. Weir

We had an experience recently which shows the difficulty that arises when we attempt to move a people from one area to another. We must keep these things in mind, and I have an appreciation of what the government is up against in its attempt to reallocate people to different types of work and in different places.
May I here, however, suggest to the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) that he give consideration to utilizing the services of these conscientious objectors in essential work, where they could be utilized in groups, under supervision. I have in mind at the moment the production of sugar beets, woodcutting, lumber mill work, and work in some of our coal mines. All these are essential requirements, and all are experiencing difficulty in securing labour.
So far as the sugar beet growers of Manitoba are concerned. I believe I may say that unless some steps are taken to assure them of a supply of labour, the sugar beet acreage in that province will be greatly reduced in the coming year. The beet growers would, I believe, be prepared to use this type of labour. They would be willing to pay to the government an agreed-upon contract price for work done. The government, on the other hand, could continue to require these people to perform a service, and, a useful service, under supervision, as it has in the past. Of course, the government would be required to provide accommodation and pay whatever compensation was decided upon, but it is doing that anyway. If it carried out the. suggestion I have made, it would only be extending that principle a little further. A similar policy might be worked out with respect to the other types of work that I have suggested, and it might be extended to other types of seasonal farm work.
I do not propose to place on the record again what Canada is accomplishing in providing men and weapons of war. This has been done already by others in a most effective manner, and I am sure that the country has now a pretty complete picture of what Canada has done in a very short period of time. I wish, however, to refer to certain other features of our production which I fear are being lost sight of but which, to me at least, are most important. These have a direct bearing upon the extent to which our man-power may be available for military service. These things were of secondary importance during the last war. We are liable to lose sight of what is being done and of what it may be necessary to do in order to maintain the flow of things we are manufacturing at the present time.

Right now our munitions and supplies are going to every theatre of war. Our ships are sailing every sea and our aircraft are to be seen in every sky. Our foodstuffs are available in ever-increasing quantities. Do we ever stop to think of what is behind this effort, the effort that Prime Minister Churchill called magnificent? This is a war that requires equipment superior to that of the enemy, and lots of it. Equipment, planes, tanks and ships are the items being called for. These things require not only men to make them, but men to keep the raw materials flowing and men to move these things to the places where they are required. To illustrate what I have in mind I should like to refer briefly to a few changes that have taken place in our production field during this war compared with the last war. In 1914 our production of aluminum was 13,000,000 pounds; in 1939 this production had risen to 150,000,000 pounds. The comparative productions in other metals are as follows:

Our oil production in 1914 was some few' (thousand barrels; to-day it is over eight and a half million barrels. Our gold production is away up as compared to what it was then. Timber production is another important item, and this has been expanded both for our own purposes and to meet the needs of Great Britain. Before the war Great Britain secured immense stocks of foodstuffs from European countries and from other parts of . the British empire. As we know and regret, these supplies have been largely cut off, thus throwing a greater responsibility upon this country to provide these essentials. Our financing arrangements with Great Britain, which have been mentioned in this house on several occasions, amount virtually to an open charge account in Canada for Great Britain. This financing must be of inestimable assistance to the mother country These things are essential, and their production must be maintained, and increased in many instances.
Keeping what I have said in mind, and adding to it our industrial production; our financial assistance; our contribution to the armed forces, to the air force, to the navy; our efforts in charitable work through the Red Cross and other services, one cannot help but realize, having regard to. our geographical position,

The Address-Mr. Gingues
that the contribution of Canada is something of which every Canadian can be justly proud.
For the moment some of these accomplishments are being lost sight of. For the time being our efforts are being overshadowed by developments elsewhere. The centre of the stage is being taken by developments on the battle fronts and the diplomatic activities in London, Washington and Moscow. Our minds are filled with what is happening in Libya, on the Pacific, at Singapore, at Hong Kong and in Russia. The success of the efforts in these far-flung battlefields nevertheless is still dependent to a very large extent upon what we as individuals do on the home front to maintain those in the front lines.
I had intended to refer to two or three other matters, but other opportunities will be provided for that. In 1940 the present government received a mandate to prosecute this war. There is no doubt that the efforts of the government were under review at that time. The people of Canada showed their confidence in the present Prime Minister in a manner unexcelled in the history of this country. When the history of this period is written I feel confident that the name of W. L. Mackenzie King will stand high among the names of the great world leaders because of the part he has played at this time. We entered this conflict determined to see it through regardless of cost, and we are still going to do that. The people of Canada are prepared for added sacrifices; they are ready to do whatever may be required of them. For the most part many are doing that already in their own quiet way, probably about as effectively as if they were under more rigid direction. All they ask is that they be told the job the government wants to have done. They are prepared to do it. The only other thing they ask of those who are directing the war effort of this country at the present time is that the burden of this terrific effort shall be distributed equitably.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join my colleagues who have already spoken in this debate in congratulating the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier) for the speech he has delivered in moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I also wish to compliment the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) on the effective manner in which he has seconded that motion.
I regret that I do not have their parliamentary experience on the occasion of my first speech in this house, for, as a matter of fact, I rise to-night for the first time since I have the honour to represent the
constituency of Sherbrooke, in order to express my views to the Parliament of this country in such an important debate.
It has been ordained by Providence that I should deliver my first speech in this house at the most critical period in the history of the world and of our country. But, Mr. Speaker, before coming to the matter which to my mind transcends all others, may I thank the good people of Sherbrooke-a constituency both agricultural and industrial, where citizens of both races give to the country the example of practical and true harmony-for the honour they have done me in selecting me as their representative in the Canadian parliament. I said that I would discuss a matter which in my opinion transcends all others, and I meant the plebiscite. Since the reading of the speech from the throne, much has been written and said about conscription of both man-power and wealth, and the subject has entailed the expenditure of much money and energy. It seems that if we had taken as much care to explain to the nation the reasons for the plebiscite this house would probably be ready to-night to vote on the main motion. But once again in Canada politics had to come before country. Conscription for overseas service is the only thing that some people have seen or wanted to see in this question. The plebiscite does not mean that we shall have conscription, either of man-power or of wealth. Mr. Speaker, the plebiscite is necessary if we wish to continue to assert and proclaim everywhere that we are fighting for the preservation of democracy, for in asking the people to release them from pledges given at the 1940 general election, the administration upholds and maintains the basic principle of democracy, which is the free expression of the people's will. Moreover, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government are acting in an honest and statesmanlike manner; they are showing once again that they do not want to imitate our enemies and break their pledged word.
The plebiscite will in no way tend to hasten or delay conscription, but it is needed because the conflict is drawing ever closer to our shores and a time may come when the Canadian government will be compelled, for the defence of our territory and our homes, to take emergency measures. Let us not forget that the dreadful scourge of war is at our very door and that Canada, our fatherland, is threatened.
Never, as I say, have we faced such a terrible threat and this government know the danger that hangs over us, they are fully

The Address-Mr. Gingues

aware of it. Such is tffe reason why, while it is still time, he is calling upon the people of Canada to appreciate the gravity of the situation and asking them to give him the confidence which he needs, not to apply conscription but simply to be ready at any time to defend Canada and carry out a total and voluntary war effort.
The situation in the Pacific is daily becoming darker, and in spite of the magnificent effort put forth by this country, to use the words of the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the threat to Canada is becoming more and more serious. It would be criminal indeed to let ourselves be lulled by over-confidence and then awaken just a little too late and find ourselves under the yoke of the enemy. This government enjoys the confidence of the people. It received a vote of confidence from the people in March, 1940, when we were already at war. The situation has worsened since then. As this government has conducted the war effort efficiently so far, the people are confident that it will do nothing to weaken that war effort, but will do all that is required for the defence of the country. That does not mean resort to conscription for overseas service, for the government will always be responsible to parliament and the people's representatives remain free to approve or reject the measures submitted to them.
For my part, I will show my confidence in the government by my vote on the main motion and I shall vote against both amendments; for I know that if I am here to-day it is not so much because of the esteem my fellow-citizens have kindly shown me as because of the fact that I was the candidate of the leader of the government, of the Prime Minister. I deem it my duty to give a vote of confidence to the present administration. And all who hesitate to show such confidence in the government play into the hands of those who would overthrow the Prime Minister and disunite us that they may rule. Alas, I know full well that in every parliament the world over are to be found elected representatives of the people for whom a renewal of their mandate is more important than the country itself. In this critical hour when danger threatens everything that we hold dear we must forget re-election and think only of the country. As far as I am concerned, even if it means an end to my political career, I will be doing my duty if my stand is such as I conceive it to be in the interest of my countrymen, my province and my country.

As the only man whom we can confidently trust is our Prime Minister, I intend supporting him by voting for the main motion. It is unfortunate that plebiscite and conscription should appear synonymous in the eyes of certain people. After the speeches heard during the present debate from government leaders as well as from some honourable members, I am convinced that there is no ground for such a conscriptionist measure. On the contrary, it would hamper our war effort.
Since the question of conscription has been raised, Mr. Speaker, I must make known my opinion on this measure and the attitude I will take if it is ever brought before us. Before taking my seat in this house, I was opposed to this measure which I considered unjust and inhuman, neither useful nor necessary. I still hold the same opinion and nothing will change my mind on this point. I oppose conscription of wealth as much as conscription of man-power, for in my opinion we are at this time making the best possible use of Canadian resources. If we stop to consider the taxes which Canadians are called upon to pay, we soon realize that taxation has reached a point beyond which we risk achieving destruction of private enterprise. The present taxes of every kind which must be paid by the humblest workingman as well as by the greatest financier, national defence tax, income tax, excess profits tax, succession duties, are all very well, but it cannot be denied that we have gone far enough and I trust the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), when presenting his next budget, will not increase unduly the burden already carried by the Canadian people and will rest content with the taxes we already have to meet. After all, we cannot ask from the taxpayer more than he can pay.
Notwithstanding all these taxes and all these measures, opposition members attack the government for being unwilling to assume their responsibilities. When has the government hesitated to assume responsibility, I ask you? Was it when they submitted their bill for the mobilization of national resources? Was it when they increased taxation, was it when they forced employers to pay cost-of-living bonuses to their employees or when they enforced that radical but necessary measure of price control?
No, Mr. Speaker, the present government never has refused to assume responsibility. Far from it. They have been wise enough to make it impossible for certain individuals to exploit for their own benefit the financial and industrial resources of the country. This

The Address-Mr. Gingues
explains perhaps the reason why a small group of men would overthrow the Prime Minister, while loudly proclaiming their would-be love of country, trying to appear more patriotic than their neighbour and endeavouring, in this critical period, to divide the Liberal party so as to obtain power and thereafter so direct our war effort that this same group of men may hold sway over the economic life of the country just like they did after the last war. The people must be cautioned against those evil persons who are ready to revive, for the workers and the farmers, the sorry policy of relief and bread lines.
I wish to state frankly, that we are fighting and we shall keep on fighting not only to defeat nazism, but also to ward off the return of disastrous conditions, to increase economic security for the worker and the farmer.
I am opposed to conscription of manpower. In the course of this debate, all kinds of sound arguments have been stated to show that this method has been a failure, but there is another reason on which I would like to dwell. This matter, Mr. Speaker, reminds me of the Canadian mothers. I wish to state that, at this particular moment, I am not speaking as the representative of Sherbrooke constituency only; I wish to speak on behalf of Canadian mothers, whether they speak French or English or any other language, provided they be Canadian. It is for them that I speak against this unfair, useless and inhuman measure; while doing so, I think of the Canadian mothers whose lives are filled with self-denial, devotion to duty, and who raise large families for their country. During the last war, the government of the day, believing that there could be no victory without conscription, enforced that method of raising men. The results are so well known that I need not recall them.
What happened since? Canadian mothers have pondered over this. In the last 25 years the birth rate has fallen to an alarming degree. If we are unfortunate enough to enforce such an unfair measure now, birth control will become more prevalent in the future and, Mr. Speaker, I claim that by the enactment of a law that would undermine the family, we would endanger the very foundation of the nation. We are fighting for the conservation of our property and the continued development of our country, for building a great Canada, a Canadian mentality, a Canadian spirit. This end will never be
44561-434 [DOT]
attained through immigration, but rather by encouraging large families, by showing that we are worthy of the great cause for which we are fighting: Christian civilization.
It behooves us, the parliament of the nation, to act in such a way that the world may gauge the depth of our sincerity. In opposing this measure for this reason based on common sense and truth, I have confidence of acting as a Christian, as a member of a Christian parliament. And whenever consription is brought up, I shall fight it with all my strength. I hope that, at the conclusion of the war, when we see the flag waving as an emblem and a guarantee of peace and freedom, then the citizens of our large cities may erect, on our public squares, not only memorials to our gallant soldiers as a reminder for generations to come, but also monuments to the Canadian mothers.
I wish to say a few words about the province of Quebec, the loyalty of which is apparently questioned by some. Have hon. members already forgotten that on October 25, 1939, the people of that province, called upon to select a government, chose the party which had had the courage to fight for the principle of participation in the war? Has there been a proper realization of the importance of that, election and has due credit been given to -those who were responsible for the result obtained? If Quebec had unfortunately turned out to be what some think it is and *had returned to power the Conservative party disguised as the "National Union" government, Canada's war effort would have been considerably weakened.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to say that on that occasion it was the Liberal party that risked everything and that it was the Liberal leaders who waged the good fight, not the leader of the opposition nor the men who to-day are seeking to divide the nation. On the contrary the whole Conservative organization of Quebec supported the "National Union ' candidates. It seems to me that on that occasion the people of Quebec gave manifest proof of their loyalty and patriotism, as they have given since at every opportunity. There are extremists in Quebec as there are elsewhere, but believe me, Mr. Speaker, their number is small in Quebec as it is small elsewhere.
If I remind the house of this action taken by my province in 1939, it is because of the important effect I believe it has had on our war effort.
Mr. Speaker, the situation is serious, danger is at our door. Let us not wait until we have to defend ourselves at Vancouver, Halifax, Quebec or Toronto. Let us join in a holy
The Address-Mr. Gingues

union, laying aside all prejudice and political passion. Let us put our trust in the best administration Canada has ever had. To those who abstain from voting on the main motion or who vote against it, I say that they are doing a disservice to their country.
As was so well said in his first speech in this house by an lion, member whom I wish to warmly congratulate, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Cote): Let all those who have lately devoted so much energy to dividing the nation now concentrate their activities on helping our war effort, and I am convinced that this effort will remain voluntary and will be able to bring us victory and peace.
The people of the United States are now using a motto which constantly reminds them that they are at war. On all sides they see posted up the words "Remember Pearl Harbor." The regretted Minister of Justice, Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe, speaking in Sherbrooke at the outset of the war, gave us a motto when he said: "One country, two languages, different religions, but only one heart." This is what we see in Canada to-day and what we will always see:
11,500,000	Canadians living side by side, speaking two languages, professing different religions, but with a single heart tending towards the one ideal-the maintenance of democracy as the unshakeable bulwark of our liberty.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I wish to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier) and the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) upon their admirable speeches in opening this debate. The experience which they obtained in England, together with their legal training, helped them much and added to the excellence of their addresses.
We have heard a great deal in this debate concerning an all-out war effort. This is a term used to indicate a balanced war effort in which our military establishments, combined with our industrial effort in the production of war equipment and material for the use of our citizens, are so balanced as to result in the greatest possible war effort of our country. This can be brought to one hundred per cent effectiveness only by a certain measure of national selective service. I would add to the criticism of the government voiced by some hon. members this one thing, that a greater proportion of national selective service might have been brought about.

Canada's war effort to-day is second to that of none of the united nations, having regard to our population. Under the leadership of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a great deal has been accomplished. I followed for many years his efforts to bring about economic cooperation between the United States and Canada, and between the British empire and the United States. I am one who believes that if this cooperation had been brought about several years ago, it would have had a steadying influence in the world and might have prevented this world war. When the history of this war is written I am sure that the work of our Prime Minister in bringing about cooperation between the great Anglo-Saxon nations will be recognized as one of the most important phases of our war effort.
Since the outbreak of the war the heads of our military, naval and air departments have given outstanding service. The figures covering the expansion in these departments have been given to the house; and I shall not repeat them. But may I say that the successful handling of Canada's financial effort by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is second to that of none of the other united nations. The excellence of his work is being recognized by the people of Canada. On February 10 the Minister of Finance spoke before the Rotary club of Montreal. In an editorial on February 11 the Montreal Star paid him this tribute:
There is, as a rule, very little in financial matters that makes for inspiration, but Mr. Ilsley's handling of his theme was not only masterly, it was inspired. And it stirred responsive emotions in the minds of all who were privileged to hear him. There were passages in his speech that reached a high measure of eloquence, but they were not mere flights of rhetoric. They came straight from the heart of a man who has shouldered a great responsibility and a tremendous task, who is conscious of the immense strain which Canada's commitments place upon the nation, but who has absolute confidence that the nation will not fail.
That is a well-earned tribute. In his speech the Minister of Finance said:
Let me tell you what I think we should aim to do: I think we should aim to make a reputation for Canadian achievement in this war which will be the talk of the world for generations, that will be the pride of ourselves, our children, and our children's children.
I agree with the sentiment there expressed. Let me add that I feel, and I believe all hon. members feel, that no sacrifice is too great for our generation to make to ensure that when those children's children take our places as citizens of this great dominion, Canada will still be Canada.

The Address-Mr. Hill
The work of our Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) sitands out as one of the greatest pieces of organization in our war effort. I know that other hon. members who belong to the engineering profession will join with me in expressing satisfaction at the splendid service given to Canada by a member of our profession. Canada was indeed fortunate that at the outbreak of the war there was a member of the cabinet so highly trained in engineering and whose later experience in industrial engineering had so fitted him for the great task of directing the reorganization of the industrial life of Canada for war. As soon as the war broke out, the minister called many of the best industrial organizers and organizations of the dominion to Ottawa. Many of these men were experts in various lines of industry, and to their credit be it said that they volunteered their services and were permitted by their companies to give their time and effort to placing the industrial life of Canada on a war footing.
There was much to be done at the start; in fact chaotic conditions existed. Canada had but one munitions plant producing war equipment. The whole industrial life of the country had to be changed from peace-time pursuits to a war-time basis. During the first year of the war many of us felt that the progress which was being made was not as great as it should be. But in changing over the entire industrial life of Canada we had to creep before we could walk and walk before we could run, and I believe we have yet to learn to run efficiently enough to enable us to win this war. If, however, one takes the actual production month by month since the beginning of the war, it will be noted that while at first we progressed in arithmetical progression, we are now going ahead in geometrical progression.
When we look at the present output of Canada in war material and farm production we realize that we are well on the way to the goal of mass production, a term which has been used for all-out efficient production. And when we look at the number of people employed on war work and the number in our army, navy and air force, we realize that we are approaching the limit of our manpower along certain lines. There is, however, one large field which, I believe, has not yet been touched; that is in the smaller centres of population in our country. I am convinced that the Minister of Munitions and Supply has organized the great centres of mass production in Ontario and Quebec so well that he may now turn his organizing ability to the smaller centres without hurting production in the larger centres; those centres will go on under their own momentum. But
in many small towns in Canada-and I know for a fact in many small towns in New Brunswick-there are many thousands of men and women who could be employed in ivar work without in any way interfering with the ordinary life of the country. I assume that the work of organizing these people, which has to do with national selective service, will be done by the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) in conjunction with the Minister of Munitions and Supply. In New Brunswick, in the smaller towns of 1,000 to 5,000 population, there are many men and women, men not eligible for war service, who are employed only part time, or employed in non-essential work. These people could be organized to advantage, and I believe it is the duty of the Minister of Munitions and Supply to give this matter his most serious attention at an early date.
In the constituency which I have the honour to represent there are four small towns with populations ranging from 1,500 to 5,000. No war work is being done for the Canadian government in any of these towns, though one small factory in one town is doing work for the British government, in the production of shell boxes. I believe this condition exists also in many small towns throughout Canada. It is just possible that the smaller communities in Quebec and Ontario have had their available labour moved to the larger centres, but that is not the case in many sections of the prairies and in eastern Canada. I know also that when the rationing of gasoline, the rationing of tires, the reduction in the use of automobiles and the reduction in tourist traffic take place, many men will be thrown out of employment in our garages and service stations. They are not men of military age. They are practical mechanics, with many years of experience in this work. These men should be most valuable in the war service of Canada, and steps should be taken at once to see that when they are thrown out of work in the spring, their services will be utilized.
In many sections of New Brunswick there is a feeling of frustration among the people because of the fact that they are not employed at something they feel is of value to the war effort of this dominion. I should like to suggest to the Minister of Munitions and Supply that one method by which this situation could be overcome would be by the appointment of an assistant, or perhaps two assistants, one of whom should be a business man, who would be located in these smaller provinces. They should be located, not in Ottawa, but in the province whose war effort they are interested in building up. Then they could be in constant touch with the local

The Address-Mr. Hill
government, and with industries throughout the province; they would know where labour could be found and could advise the minister as to the steps that should be taken to place industries in suitable locations, where these men might be given employment in active war work.
I have been told that the unit cost of production is far greater in these small centres than in the mass-production centres. I believe this is true, up to the point where you have to bring labour from other sections or other provinces to these mass-production centres. The moment you do this, you have to add the cost of transporting these men. They have to leave their families behind; they have to maintain themselves in these centres. Already the government has embarked upon housing schemes for these workers. If it would take all these costs, which are costs to this country, into consideration, I believe it would find that the cost of extending production in these mass-production centres is greater than would be the cost of production in the smaller places. Then, again, suppose we are not getting the production we should get in these smaller centres, and these people are not taken to the larger centres. This means that we lose a certain amount of production. Supposing a shell produced in a smaller centre cost $2 instead of $1.75. Many battles have been lost in this war because of lack of equipment, and I would rather have a $2 shell than none at all.
I would recommend to the minister that he give most serious consideration to this matter, for I believe that production can be stepped up to a far greater extent by this method in the coming year than by the further extension *of facilities which already exist in the more thickly populated centres of production.
I have some information here which comes from a quarterly review of public affairs published by Dalhousie university, in the city of Halifax. The Minister of Munitions and Supply was formerly professor of engineering at that university, so he should have some regard for these suggestions. In this publication I find that on a per capita basis, in the maritime provinces only one-third of the amount of money has been spent on war products that has been spent in the whole of Canada, When this matter was brought to the attention of the government it was said that in the maritimes we did not have the industrial equipment with which to do this work; but according to this report, having regard to each thousand dollars invested in industrial plant, we still have only one-half as much money being spent in the maritimes as is being spent in the rest of Canada. The greatest injustice to New Brunswick is shown 
in the final figures, which have to do with grants in connection with the construction of industrial plants in Canada. I find that New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island obtained only one-fourth of one per cent of the total amount spent for this purpose throughout Canada, though this district has five per cent of the population of this country. This, I think, accounts for the fact that we are not getting war orders in that part of the country, and for the further fact that there is a feeling of frustration among the workers there.
All hon. members must realize that there is a limit to the man-power that can be secured for military purposes. This is governed by the number of men in our population who are physically fit and between certain ages. The only way by which any increase can be brought about is by new classes coming of age or by the extension of the age limit. There is a grave question in my mind as to whether the extension of the age limit will not result in men being placed in military service who could be far more useful to our war effort in the production of military equipment. While this is true of the men available for war purposes, I am not one of those who believe that our production of materials, equipment and food for the carrying on of our war effort will ever reach a maximum. If this war should go on for another ten years, I think every hon. member is convinced that our production at the end of that period will be greater than at any intermediate stage. The reason is that while our man- and woman-power available for industrial production may reach its limit, the improvement in machines, the bringing into production of more electrical power, and the use of more efficient methods of production will each year enable the same number of employees to produce larger quantities of goods. Then, again, as the necessity arises, greater effort will be made by the man-power employed in the production of equipment.
A great deal has been said in this house with reference to the immediate conscription of man-power for overseas service as an absolute essential to an all-out war effort. After listening to the enlistment records as given by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), I am quite convinced that voluntary enlistment has not failed; in fact, that it has not yet faltered. I am one of those who believe that an army of men enlisted for overseas service of their own free will is a far more effective army than one of men who had to be enlisted by compulsion. I also believe that as long as our voluntary enlistment method does not fail, we should not bring in compulsory service for overseas. I believe, too, that an army for home defence

The Address-Mr. Hill
obtained by compulsory service is just as effective in its own land as one which is formed by voluntary enlistment. My reason for making that statement is that the men have the incentive of fighting on their own soil. Therefore I believe that conscription for home service would produce an able and efficient army for the defence of our shores, should that defence be required.
The county and province I represent in the house has, I am proud to say, shown voluntary enlistments for overseas service equal to those of any other part of the Dominion of Canada. In proportion to its population, New Brunswick has the best record for voluntary enlistment in the army, for active service overseas, of any military district.

speechtext:
Yes, I believe it is; but I am speaking of military districts. The voluntary enlistment record of New Brunswick, for all branches of the service, including the navy and the air force, stands with three other districts as being highest in the dominion. Every time recruits have been called for, or a drive has been put on to increase the numbers of those enlisted for active service overseas, the county of Charlotte, and the province of New Brunswick as a whole, have always filled their quota. In New Brunswick we have a mixed population, comprising the two great races of Canada. Approximately one-third of our population in New Brunswick is of French origin. I know all hon. members from New Brunswick, on both the government and opposition benches, and including the house leader of the official opposition party, the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) will agree with me when I say that we are justly proud of the record of our French citizens, as far as enlistments for active service for overseas are concerned. They have kept that record up, man for man, according to their population, along with their Englishspeaking compatriots in our province, and I know that all citizens of New Brunswick are proud of this fact. When a further call is made to bring up the strength of our overseas service, New Brunswick will not be lacking.
We have heard a great deal in the house about the conscription of wealth. I say that we have already started on the conscription of wealth. When a country which produced only $10,000,000 from income tax during the whole four years of the last great war, now produces between S600,000,000 and $700,000,000 from the same source within twelve months, we are certainly on the road to the conscription of wealth. It is my firm conviction that when the Minister of Finance brings down his next budget, hon. members and the people of Canada generally will be satisfied that we are increasing the conscription of wealth in Canada.
The government proposes a plebiscite of the people, not to decide the question with respect to compulsory national selective service, but to determine whether the people are prepared to release the government and private members from pledges given during the last election campaign. In that campaign the Prime Minister and other Liberal leaders pledged their party that conscription of men for overseas service would not be brought into force without consulting the people. The leader of the National government party went farther, and pledging his party and himself, stated that he was unalterably and absolutely opposed to conscription. He based his opposition on the fact that during the last war he had supported conscription, and supported the Union government; but he claimed that conscription was a failure at the time of the last war, and that it stirred up so much misunderstanding throughout the country that it had retarded Canada's war effort. He added that for that reason, and because it was the duty of a public man to uphold the unity of Canada, he was absolutely opposed to conscription of men for overseas service. I believe that that speech pledged his party and his supporters to no conscription for overseas service.
The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) was reported in the press during the campaign as stating that his party was unalterably opposed to conscription of men for overseas service. In view of the definite pledges given to the people at that time, binding practically every hon. member, I cannot see how any hon. member can object to referring this matter to the people for their decision, as promised by the Prime Minister. The people are to be asked whether they are prepared to release the government and every member of parliament from the pledges given, and to place full responsibility for every action and decision
6S0
The Address-Mr. Hill

with reference to our war effort squarely on the shoulders of their representatives in parliament.
I, for one, Mr. Speaker, believe that pledges made to the people should be carried out, and I have confidence that the decision of the majority of people in Canada will be in the best interests of the country as a whole. I have confidence that the people of the constituency of Charlotte, which I have the honour to represent, are prepared to make any sacrifice to win the war. If they will by their vote place the responsibility on me as their representative to take decisions on the serious problems which come before parliament-and these problems will be serious, before the war is ended, problems which I believe will affect the entire way of life in the country-I am prepared to assume that responsibility, and do what I believe is in the best interests of Canada, and the war effort of the dominion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although we have now reached the nineteenth sitting of the house no one has yet forgotten the eloquence and the remarkable reasoning of the mover, the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier), and the seconder, the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald), of the address in reply to the speech from the throne and, after so many others, I also wish to offer my congratulations. Brevity is imperative at this stage and I will be brief.
The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has moved an amendment containing but one point-and it is not striking for its novelty-namely conscription of Canadians for overseas service. His speech, fair enough in form, was spoiled by two or three partisan tirades and certain passages, which I really find quite insulting, where he quoted Lincoln to show off as cowards and slackers those who favour voluntary enlistment. I had attached little importance at first to this quotation from Lincoln, as we are in the habit -save perhaps for the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot)-to overlook many things from the leader of the opposition. But since hearing this same quotation from the lips of the honourable member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), I could not overcome the urge to protest.
Needless to state that I do not hold anything against Abraham Lincoln, who never spoke a word about us.
The generous soul of the great emancipator must be very sad when Tories use his words to insult people whose only' crime is to be loyal to their country first and above all. Lincoln
[Mr. Hill.)
fought to preserve unity in his country; but our Tories are doing their utmost to divide theirs.
No, French Canadians are not cowards because they are opposed to conscription for overseas service. On the contrary, they endure sarcasm, abuse and severe retaliation on the part of a fanatical press and others. They accepted conscription for the defence of our country without a moment's hesitation; they will accept it also for the defence of the continent. They have approved the policy of voluntary participation and have generously contributed to Canada's war effort outside the country.
Why did they do it? To please their compatriots of Anglo-Saxon origin who were naturally and spontaneously drawn in this war by the call of blood. We certainly hate nazism, that German form of superimperialism which is repugnant to our Catholic mind; but such ideological considerations would have been insufficient to make us vote for war. The reason why we voted with our fellow Canadians of Anglo-Saxon origin, whose feelings we understand and appreciate, resides in a true desire to cooperate with them. Since then, we have been cooperating with them throughout. But we are not ready to accept conscription of man-power for overseas service, which would only result in disrupting the country without adding anything worthwhile to our war effort. Our English-speaking fellow Canadians should, instead of pressing this point, abide by the well defined attitude which prevailed when we entered the war. When the defence of Canada is at stake-the urgency of which is daily becoming greater-French Canadians are prepared to make all necessary sacrifices. I am one of those who believe that we should have larger home-defence forces, better equipped and better trained than those we now have. Too many people are apparently obsessed by the idea of sending overseas as many of our soldiers as we can. It is a fixed idea with them. And in a changing world like ours fixed ideas must be looked upon with a great deal of suspicion.
People who have neither learned nor forgotten anything since the last war are dangerous people.
How much nearer to my heart is the leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) who so ably manages to analyse fresh developments and the changing aspects of the world drama, and who knows how to draw from them the conclusions of real interest to us. When the history of this country is written, his prudence and circumspection will assume a legendary character. And it is this sage among sages

The Address-Mr. Authier
who has been attacked and vilified throughout the country by a press in the pay of narrow and fanatical partisans, worthy successors of those who, in the last century, set fire to the Canadian parliament buildings and cast stones at a noble representative of the King in Canada, the father of our constitutional liberties. Fortunately, the majority of the people see clearly in the matter and, on February 9, those enemies of the Canadian mind already reaped part of the punishment they deserve and which will surely be visited upon them.
I anticipate with much pleasure the forthcoming entrance into this house of the victors in the recent elections: my old friend the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Saint-Laurent); my former colleague in the Quebec provincial legislature, the member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Fauteux) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), whose special ability is everywhere acknowledged; and, finally, the vanquisher of the Tory leader in the constituency of York South. Since this latter victory. I think less unkindly of Toronto.
Incidentally, I wish to tell the members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation that I share many of their views in the field of economics. I shall not, however, support the amendment proposed by their leader. He goes too far. We cannot, in the midst of a war crisis, risk so radical an economic and social revolution. But the after-war will bring a new order which will surely borrow something, perhaps a good deal, from the doctrine to which they adhere. With the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen) I suggest to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well) and to the leader of the official opposition that they withdraw their amendments so as to make the adoption of the address unanimous, as it should be.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot resume my seat without saying a few words about the proposed plebiscite and a few other questions which command the attention of my electors and of parliament.
The war takes a new turn from month to month, and sometimes oftener. We must be prepared for any emergency.
I said a moment ago that I would have no objection to our conscripts serving for the defence of the American continent. But it would be necessary to modify the existing act for that purpose. The Prime Minister, wishing to be true to his promise and to respect the will of the people, is asking by means of a plebiscite to be freed from all obstacles that would prevent him from adopting measures which the government might deem necessary.
I have enough confidence in the Prime Minister to support him on this occasion. All measures submitted to the house later on will be judged on their merits. Moreover, the electors will be free to vote according to the dictates of their conscience on this plebiscite.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) is asking the Canadian people to subscribe to a $600,000,000 loan. I wish him all the success possible, but I must say frankly that the circumstances are not as favourable in my district on this occasion as they were for the preceding loan. Rumours have been heard that the gold mines may soon be forced to curtail their production. Miners and those living in mining towns, alarmed at such rumours, will naturally keep their savings instead of buying government bonds. They are likely to forget that government bonds are for all practical purposes like money in the bank.
I cannot see how the country would benefit by closing gold mines producing at the rate of $200,000,000 a year. Even if the United States were to suspend all gold imports, it would still be to the advantage of Canada to build up reserves for the future. A reserve of two billion dollars in Canada would be the equivalent of that existing in the United States. That would mean ten years' production for our mines.
Logging is also an important industry in the section of Quebec which I represent. I read in the press recently that the price of pulpwood was fixed by the timber controller. By unanimous request of the. people of Quebec, the government of this province are investigating prices and sales conditions of pulpwood, in order that reasonable prices may obtain in certain sections of the province where wood is practically given away for nothing. In fact, in my constituency settlers clearing new land several miles from the railroad have often had to deliver their wood, with the bark removed, on the car for $6 and $7 a cord. This price represents poor wages for cutting and barking, very little for hauling and nothing at all for the wood itself. There can be no justification for the maintenance of such unfair prices, and I hope that the timber controller will cooperate with the provincial administration, which is willing to remove such abuses.
In his amendment to the address, the leader of the opposition referred to the necessity of preparing for the after-war period. Everyone knows that the government has the question under consideration. In a statement subsequent to the speech from the throne, the Prime Minister referred to colonization as a means to that end.

The Address-Mr. Auihier

I wish, Mr. Speaker, to recall that I have been living for thirty years in the colonization district which I have the honour to represent in this house. When I first settled in that part of the country, there were only a few squatters, possibly a dozen families in the neighbourhood, and the labourers working on the construction of the Transcontinental railway. One hundred miles from that railroad, on the shores of lake Temiskaming, there were half a dozen parishes, and less than ten thousand people all told. According to the figures of the latest census, the two constituencies Temiscamingue and Abitibi, forming the northwestern portion of the province of Quebec, now have a population of 110,000. The fact that their population increased by
100.000	in thirty years is chiefly due to land settlement, which ought to go on for a long time to come in that vast area. I do not say that the best tillable land in Canada is to be found there, lest I should distress my right-hand neighbour the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Sissons). But it is the last extensive land settlement area that remains in the province of Quebec. May this fact not be forgotten in the post-war programme. It would be advisable to do some preliminary work there. The Canadian government has for some years extended assistance for the building of roads in mining areas. A similar policy should be adopted with a view to opening or completing certain main roads leading into our best remaining lands.
During this session I shall no doubt have another opportunity to bring up this subject which is of vital importance in any post-war planning. I have no objection to the government helping the farmers of the west, the industries of central Canada and the fishermen of our coastal provinces, but they should also encourage the efforts of the settlers in the newly opened lands of Quebec, who are constantly extending our agricultural area through hard and often thankless work, for which they deserve all the more credit.
Mr. JOSEPH H. LECLERC (Shefford): Mr. Speaker, as very few minutes remain before adjournment, I shall be brief. I have but a few remarks to make, anyhow.
At this stage of the debate on the address, which has now lasted for three weeks, I must say how much I admire your patience in listening to the same arguments put forth in different tones. I intend being very brief as I do not approve of indefinitely travelling beaten roads. Believing, however, that the people of my constituency wish to know what stand their representative is taking, I wish

to say a few words on the subject of conscription, which is so much in the public mind at the present.
Mr. Speaker, there is no need for me to play both ends against the middle, as I expect nothing from politics and- my sole ambition is to remain ever faithful to those whom I represent.

I do not hesitate to say that the electors in my constituency, in my province and in the country have much more confidence at the present moment in the Right Hon. Mackenzie King than in the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen who has just met defeat in York South. All Liberal members, including the dissentients, state that their confidence is far greater in the King administration than in any other.
I am not a real politician, Mr. Speaker, but it does seem to me that you will readily understand how illogical those dissenting Liberals are. Should we all follow their example and vote with the Conservatives against adopting the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the present government would be overthrown only to be succeeded' by a union government. For my part, I do not feel inclined to present the electors of Shefford constituency with such an offering. Has not the Liberal party just won four victories? This is a clear proof of the confidence the electors still place in the hon. Prime Minister. So that my position will leave no doubt whatever, I wish to state that I am personally opposed to conscription for overseas service for many reasons. The first is that I took this pledge at the last election and if there is anything I wish above all else, it is to continue to deserve the respect of my compatriots. A second reason is that, at the present time, events are taking a disquieting turn and in spite of what certain strategists, with nothing but defeats to their credit so far, might say, I feel that the sending of troops to foreign lands becomes more and more a reckless adventure.
Mr. Speaker, after this explanation, which I believe is clear enough, I shall add that it is not my intention, in constituencies which I do not represent, of holding meetings that might stir emotions in a time when composure and moderation are desirable. I do not look upon myself as the saviour of my race and I do not take myself seriously enough to assume leadership of a new party.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) has

The Address-Mr. Leclerc
assumed leadership of the Canadian party; however, noblesse oblige; will he prove equal to the task? Using the expression this hon. . leader has coined to designate his humble colleagues, I trust his "followers" in the future will be sufficient in number to insure greater success for him than at the last election.
I could add much more, but I said I would be brief. The electors of Ontario, along with those of my province, have rejected the ultra-conscriptionists. Common sense has prevailed. The electors of those constituencies have done good work for national unity and I congratulate them. Therefore, for the sake of unity, I shall not rehash the old or the new stories; 1 shall follow the advice of the well-meaning people and remain calm and moderate, so as to assuage the bad feelings all too prevalent.
Mr. Speaker, before I conclude my remarks I want to make a request to the government concerning farmers' sons who, though indispensable on the farm, are called for military service. At the present time, we experience all kinds of difficulties when we try to obtain even short postponements for those who are necessary on the farm the whole year around. The mobilization act should be amended so that farmers' sons who have never left the farm and bona fide farm workers could obtain an indefinite postponement. I maintain that the farmer who owns fifteen or twenty milch cows, not taking into account his other live stock-yearlings, hogs, et cetera-and a maple bush, never enjoys free time from one end of the year to the other. A farmer who has to look after twenty-five or thirty milch cows, even if he enjoys perfect health, cannot do all his work without the aid of at least two helpers. Whether these helpers are his own sons or hired men, they are absolutely needed for the operation of his farm. In 1941 there was a labour shortage. In 1942 the situation appears to be getting worse, with indications of a smaller agricultural production. The government is aware that England, whose people are now on short rations, needs all that we can produce on our farms.
I wish to point out that I have received no requests for postponement from men of the town of Granby and that those I have received from farmers' sons are legitimate. We are at present obliged to parley with the registrars 'who apparently know very little about farming.
Needless to say that the production of foodstuffs is just as essential as that of arms and munitions. The government should therefore leave the farm workers on the farm and have the mobilization act amended so that farmers' sons absolutely needed on the farm may obtain an indefinite postponement.
